plain_definition: Deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA, is the chemical that carries the inherited instructions used by almost every living organism. It is built from four chemical letters strung along two strands that wind around each other in a double helix. The order of those letters stores information that cells read to build proteins and to decide when each gene is switched on. Cells copy their DNA before dividing, so the instructions pass to the next generation of cells.
technical_explanation: DNA is a polymer of deoxyribonucleotides, each made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine. Sugars and phosphates form the backbone; the bases project inwards and pair specifically, adenine with thymine and cytosine with guanine, so the two antiparallel strands are complementary. That complementarity underlies both semi-conservative replication and every laboratory method that depends on hybridisation, including polymerase chain reaction, probe-based assays and sequencing by synthesis. In eukaryotes most DNA sits in the nucleus, packaged with histones into chromatin and condensed into chromosomes, with a much smaller circular genome in mitochondria. Only a minority of human DNA encodes protein; the remainder includes regulatory elements, non-coding RNA genes, repetitive sequence and segments whose function is still being characterised. A practical limitation is that sequence alone does not reveal function: identifying a stretch of DNA tells you its letters, not whether it is transcribed in a given tissue, nor what the consequence of altering it would be. Chemical modifications such as methylation and the surrounding chromatin state also shape how the same sequence behaves in different cells.
practical_example: A laboratory extracting DNA from whole blood lyses the cells, digests protein, and binds the nucleic acid to a silica column before eluting it in buffer. The scientist then measures absorbance ratios and fragment size to judge purity and integrity, because degraded or protein-contaminated DNA performs poorly in library preparation. Only material passing those checks goes forward to sequencing.
common_misunderstanding: A common belief is that DNA is a fixed blueprint that dictates outcomes directly. Sequence constrains what a cell can make, but gene expression, epigenetic modification, developmental timing and environment all shape the result. It is also wrong to speak of a single normal human DNA sequence: variation between individuals and populations is ordinary, and reference sequences are conventions rather than ideals.

plain_definition: Ribonucleic acid, or RNA, is a nucleic acid closely related to DNA that cells use to carry and act on genetic information. It is usually single-stranded and uses the base uracil where DNA uses thymine. Some RNA molecules carry the instructions for making a protein, while others help build proteins, regulate which genes are active, or form part of the cell's machinery.
technical_explanation: RNA is a polymer of ribonucleotides in which the sugar is ribose and the four bases are adenine, cytosine, guanine and uracil. The extra hydroxyl group on ribose makes RNA chemically less stable than DNA, which is why RNA work demands cold chains, RNase-free reagents and prompt stabilisation of samples. Functionally RNA is diverse: messenger RNA conveys coding sequence from gene to ribosome; transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA carry out translation; small nuclear RNAs drive splicing; and microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs modulate transcript stability and transcription. Many viruses, including influenza and coronaviruses, use RNA as their genetic material, so pathogen surveillance frequently begins with reverse transcription of viral RNA to complementary DNA. Because RNA abundance reflects cellular state rather than inherited sequence alone, transcriptome measurements are context-dependent: the same genome yields different RNA profiles in different tissues, at different times and under different stimuli. That context dependence is informative but also a limitation, since an RNA measurement without matched metadata is difficult to interpret.
practical_example: A surveillance laboratory receiving nasopharyngeal swabs extracts total nucleic acid, reverse-transcribes any viral RNA, and runs a quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Samples held too long at room temperature give weak or absent signal because the RNA has degraded, so the team records collection and receipt times alongside each result and repeats testing when transport conditions were poor.
common_misunderstanding: People often assume RNA is simply a disposable copy of DNA. Messenger RNA does act as an intermediate, but most cellular RNA is never translated and instead performs structural, catalytic or regulatory work. Assuming that RNA levels equal protein levels is a second error: transcript abundance and protein abundance correlate only loosely, because translation and protein turnover are separately regulated.

plain_definition: A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for making a product the cell uses, most often a protein but sometimes a functional RNA molecule. Each gene sits at a particular place on a chromosome and usually includes signals that control when and where it is switched on. People carry two copies of most genes, one inherited from each parent.
technical_explanation: A gene is conventionally defined as a genomic interval that is transcribed and gives rise to one or more functional products. In practice the boundaries are set by annotation: a gene model in a database such as Ensembl lists exons, introns, transcription start sites and alternative transcripts, and these models are revised as evidence accumulates. Protein-coding genes are a minority of annotated human genes; the catalogue also includes RNA genes and pseudogenes. Alternative splicing, alternative promoters and alternative polyadenylation mean that one locus can yield several transcripts with different coding potential, so a gene name alone is an imprecise description of what is actually expressed. Clinically this matters because variant interpretation depends on which transcript is treated as canonical, and laboratories therefore quote a specific transcript identifier alongside nomenclature for any reported variant. Gene names also change: approved symbols are curated and historical synonyms persist in older literature. A further limitation is that assigning function to a gene usually rests on experiments in particular cell types or model organisms, so inferences about its role in human tissue should be stated as inference rather than fact.
practical_example: A diagnostic laboratory reporting a variant in a cardiomyopathy panel writes the gene symbol, the reference transcript and the variant in standard nomenclature. A referring clinician who sees only the gene symbol cannot tell which transcript was used, and because exon numbering differs between transcripts, the transcript identifier is what makes the report reproducible in another laboratory.
common_misunderstanding: Many readers picture one gene producing one protein and one trait. Most genes produce several transcripts, most traits involve many genes together with environment, and a single gene can contribute to several unrelated phenotypes. Describing a gene as the gene for a disease is similarly misleading, since the gene exists in everyone and only particular variants within it are associated with disease.

plain_definition: A genome is the complete set of genetic material in an organism or a cell. For a person this means all the DNA in the nucleus, inherited from both parents, plus the small separate genome inside mitochondria. The genome includes genes and the much larger amount of DNA between and around them that helps control how genes behave.
technical_explanation: The human nuclear genome comprises roughly three billion base pairs distributed across twenty-two autosome pairs and the sex chromosomes, together with a circular mitochondrial genome of about sixteen and a half kilobases. Sequencing a genome means determining that sequence from an individual sample; interpreting it means comparing the result against a reference assembly and a catalogue of known variation. Successive reference assemblies have improved completeness, and a telomere-to-telomere assembly resolved repetitive regions that short-read methods had left as gaps, while pangenome resources represent multiple haplotypes instead of a single linear coordinate system. This matters because a single linear reference built largely from a few donors represents global human variation unevenly, and variants common in under-represented populations are more likely to be missed or misclassified. Genome in common usage also denotes the organism-level sequence of a pathogen, where assemblies are small enough to generate routinely during outbreaks. A limitation of whole-genome data is coverage of difficult regions: segmental duplications, long repeats and high-GC sequence remain harder to call confidently, so a genome described as complete is complete only within the limits of the technology used.
practical_example: A national reference laboratory assembling bacterial genomes from an outbreak compares each isolate with the others rather than with a distant reference strain. Doing so lets them count the small number of differing sites that separate isolates and judge whether cases form a plausible transmission cluster, a question that genome-wide comparison can answer but single-gene typing cannot.
common_misunderstanding: It is often assumed that there is one human genome and that sequencing reveals everything about a person. Each individual carries millions of differences from any reference, and reference assemblies are coordinate conventions, not ideal sequences. Sequencing also does not read every base equally well, and the clinical meaning of most variation found remains unknown.

plain_definition: A chromosome is a long molecule of DNA wound around proteins and packaged so that it fits inside a cell and can be moved reliably when the cell divides. Human cells typically carry forty-six chromosomes arranged in twenty-three pairs, with one member of each pair inherited from each parent. Chromosomes become visible under a microscope when a cell is dividing.
technical_explanation: Eukaryotic chromosomes are linear DNA molecules organised with histones into nucleosomes and higher-order chromatin, with a centromere that anchors the spindle and telomeres that cap each end. Human somatic cells are diploid with twenty-two autosome pairs plus two sex chromosomes, while gametes are haploid. Chromosome structure is functionally important: compaction state influences transcription, and three-dimensional folding brings distant regulatory elements close to promoters. Changes in chromosome number or structure are detectable by karyotyping, fluorescence in situ hybridisation, chromosomal microarray and, increasingly, by sequencing-based copy-number analysis. Bacterial chromosomes differ substantially, typically being circular, lacking histones and often accompanied by plasmids that can be gained or lost. A practical limitation of chromosome-level analysis is resolution: classical karyotyping detects rearrangements of several megabases but misses smaller imbalances, whereas array and sequencing methods detect much smaller events yet may be ambiguous about whether two segments are joined, so methods are frequently combined.
practical_example: A cytogenetics laboratory investigating recurrent pregnancy loss cultures cells, arrests them in metaphase and examines banded chromosomes. A balanced reciprocal translocation seen in one partner would not change the total amount of DNA present, which is precisely why a copy-number array alone could miss it and why the microscope-based method retains a role.
common_misunderstanding: A frequent misunderstanding is that chromosomes are the X-shaped bodies drawn in textbooks at all times. That shape appears only in dividing cells, after replication has produced two sister chromatids; for most of the cell cycle chromosomes are extended chromatin fibres. It is also incorrect to equate the sex chromosomes with a person's gender identity or social role.

plain_definition: An allele is one of the alternative versions of a sequence found at a particular place in the genome. Because people inherit one copy of each chromosome from each parent, an individual carries two alleles at most positions, which may be identical or different. Alleles can differ by a single letter or by a larger stretch of sequence.
technical_explanation: Formally an allele is a specific sequence state at a defined locus, whether that locus is a single base, a short tandem repeat, a structural segment or a whole haplotype block. Population genomics describes loci by allele frequency, and frequency is always relative to a sampled population rather than to humanity as a whole, so an allele that is common in one ancestry group may be rare in another. In diagnostic practice a laboratory reports the alleles observed and, where phasing is available, whether two variants lie on the same or opposite copies of a gene, a distinction that changes the interpretation of recessive conditions. Pharmacogenomics uses a star-allele system in which named haplotypes of genes such as CYP2D6 capture combinations of variants that together predict enzyme activity. Limitations arise from detection: short-read methods resolve some alleles poorly, especially in repetitive or paralogous regions, and an untyped allele is not the same as an absent one.
practical_example: A laboratory testing a family for a recessive condition finds two different variants in the same gene in the affected child. Only by testing the parents, or by using a method that reads both variants on one DNA molecule, can the team establish whether the variants sit on opposite chromosome copies, which is what the recessive interpretation requires.
common_misunderstanding: People often assume alleles come in a normal version and a mutant version. A reference sequence simply records what one set of donors carried, and the reference allele is not necessarily the more common or the healthier one. Allele frequencies also differ between populations for reasons of history and demography, which says nothing about the merit of any group.

plain_definition: A genotype is the particular combination of alleles an individual carries at one or more places in the genome. It can describe a single position, such as which two letters a person has at one site, or a set of positions across many genes. Genotype is determined by inheritance and, unlike many observable traits, does not usually change during life.
technical_explanation: Genotyping measures sequence state at defined positions, whereas sequencing reads a region without prior commitment to which positions will be informative. Array-based genotyping interrogates a fixed, pre-selected set of markers cheaply and reproducibly, and imputation against a reference panel can infer additional untyped sites, though accuracy falls for rare variants and for populations poorly represented in the panel. Genotype is reported per locus as homozygous for one allele, heterozygous, or hemizygous where only one copy exists, as on the X chromosome in males. In diploid analysis, genotype calls carry quality metrics such as read depth and genotype quality, and low-coverage positions produce no-calls rather than reference calls, a distinction that must be preserved in downstream analysis. Somatic genotypes in tumours differ from the germline genotype of the same person, so a tumour-only test cannot by itself distinguish inherited from acquired variants. Genotype also underdetermines phenotype: penetrance, modifier loci, epigenetic state and environment all intervene.
practical_example: A research team genotyping participants on an array obtains a set of marker calls and imputes additional sites against a reference panel. For participants of African ancestry the panel contains fewer matching haplotypes, so imputation confidence is lower at many positions, and the analysts filter on imputation quality before testing for association rather than treating all sites as equally reliable.
common_misunderstanding: A common error is to treat a missing genotype call as evidence that a person carries the reference allele. No-calls mean the assay produced no reliable result, which is different from a negative finding. A related error is reading a genotype as a prediction of a trait; most genotypes shift probabilities rather than determining outcomes.

plain_definition: A phenotype is any observable or measurable characteristic of an organism, from eye colour and height to blood test values, disease status and how someone responds to a medicine. Phenotypes arise from the combined action of genetic variation, developmental processes and environment. Because a phenotype has to be measured, how it is defined and recorded affects what any study can conclude.
technical_explanation: In genomic research the phenotype is the dependent variable, and its definition usually limits a study more than the genetic data do. Phenotypes may be binary, such as the presence of a diagnosis; quantitative, such as a laboratory measurement; or composite, derived from coded health records. Harmonising phenotypes across cohorts is difficult because diagnostic criteria, coding practice and access to care differ between sites and over time, and misclassification dilutes association signals. Structured vocabularies such as the Human Phenotype Ontology support consistent description of clinical features, which is important in rare disease where matching patients on precise features drives diagnosis. Deep phenotyping, meaning detailed longitudinal measurement, increases power but raises cost and privacy considerations. Phenotypes also vary in heritability, and a measurable family resemblance does not identify which genes are involved or imply that environment is unimportant. Expressivity and penetrance describe how the same genotype can produce phenotypes of different severity, or none at all.
practical_example: A rare disease team recording a child's features uses standardised ontology terms rather than free text. When those coded features are matched against other centres, a second child with overlapping terms and a variant in the same gene is identified, which strengthens the evidence that the gene is relevant and would have been missed had the descriptions remained in narrative form.
common_misunderstanding: It is tempting to assume that a strong genetic contribution to a phenotype means it is fixed. Heritability is a population statistic describing variance in a particular setting, not a statement about any individual, and it can change when the environment changes. Equally, an absent phenotype does not prove the absence of a relevant variant, because penetrance is often incomplete.

plain_definition: A locus is a specific location in the genome, described by the chromosome it sits on and its position along that chromosome. A locus can be as small as a single base or as large as a whole gene or region. The plural is loci. Giving a locus precisely requires stating which reference assembly the coordinates refer to.
technical_explanation: A locus is defined by genomic coordinates, and coordinates are meaningful only with respect to a named assembly, because positions shift between assembly versions. Analysts therefore record the assembly alongside any coordinate and convert between assemblies explicitly rather than assuming equivalence. Loci may be described functionally as gene loci, regulatory loci or association loci. In genome-wide association studies a reported locus is usually a region of linkage disequilibrium rather than a causal base, so the lead marker marks a neighbourhood in which the causal variant may lie, and fine-mapping is required before any gene is implicated. In pathogen genomics, loci are the typing targets of schemes such as multilocus sequence typing, where defined gene fragments are compared across isolates. A practical limitation is that paralogous and repetitive sequence can make locus assignment ambiguous: reads from one region may map to another, producing apparent variants that are artefacts of position rather than of sequence.
practical_example: An analyst receives a variant list in coordinates from an older human assembly and lifts it over to the current one before comparing with a clinical database. Two variants fail to convert because the surrounding region was reorganised between assemblies, so the analyst inspects those positions manually instead of silently dropping them from the comparison.
common_misunderstanding: A locus is often confused with a gene. Many loci lie outside genes entirely, in regulatory or intergenic sequence, and an association signal at a locus does not identify which gene it acts on. A further error is quoting coordinates without the assembly version, which makes a position ambiguous and can send a reader to the wrong part of the genome.

plain_definition: A nucleotide is the basic building block of DNA and RNA. Each one has three parts: a sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing base. Nucleotides join end to end to form long chains, and the order of their bases carries genetic information. DNA uses the bases adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine, while RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.
technical_explanation: Nucleotides consist of a pentose sugar, deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA, linked to a phosphate and to a purine or pyrimidine base. Adenine and guanine are purines; cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines. Polymerisation proceeds through phosphodiester bonds between the three-prime hydroxyl of one sugar and the five-prime phosphate of the next, giving each strand a defined directionality that governs how polymerases and nucleases act. Free nucleoside triphosphates serve both as substrates for synthesis and as energy carriers in the cell. Sequencing chemistries exploit nucleotide chemistry directly: reversible terminators halt extension after each incorporation, while chain-terminating dideoxynucleotides underpin Sanger sequencing, and nanopore methods instead read the ionic current perturbation caused by passing bases. Nucleotide counts provide the standard units for genome description, with base pairs for double-stranded DNA and bases for single-stranded molecules. Chemical modification of bases, such as cytosine methylation or oxidative damage, changes behaviour without changing the nominal sequence and can be misread as variation if not handled deliberately.
practical_example: A technician preparing a sequencing library checks fragment size and the concentration of input DNA in nanograms. Too little input forces extra amplification cycles, which increases duplicate reads and can introduce errors that resemble low-frequency variants, so the laboratory sets a minimum input threshold rather than processing every sample regardless of quantity.
common_misunderstanding: Nucleotide, nucleoside and base are often used interchangeably. A nucleoside is sugar plus base; adding one or more phosphates makes a nucleotide; the base alone is only the nitrogenous ring system. Confusing them matters when reading reagent specifications, where dideoxynucleotides, deoxynucleotides and nucleoside analogues behave very differently in a reaction.

plain_definition: A base pair is two nucleotide bases on opposite strands of a double-stranded nucleic acid that are held together by hydrogen bonds. In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine. Because of this fixed pairing, each strand carries the information needed to rebuild the other. Base pairs are also the standard unit for measuring the length of a DNA sequence.
technical_explanation: Watson-Crick base pairing joins adenine to thymine through two hydrogen bonds and cytosine to guanine through three, which is why sequences rich in cytosine and guanine melt at higher temperatures and behave differently in amplification and capture. In RNA, adenine pairs with uracil, and non-canonical pairings such as guanine-uracil wobble allow the folded structures that give functional RNAs their shapes. The abbreviation bp denotes a single base pair, with kilobase, megabase and gigabase used for larger spans, and lengths of single-stranded molecules are quoted in bases rather than base pairs. Complementary pairing is the physical basis of hybridisation-based methods: probe design, primer specificity, target capture and melting-curve analysis all depend on predictable duplex stability. A limitation is that predicted and observed hybridisation behaviour can diverge, because secondary structure, mismatches near the three-prime end of a primer, salt concentration and repetitive sequence all alter performance, which is why assays are validated empirically rather than designed on sequence rules alone.
practical_example: A laboratory designing primers for an amplicon scheme finds that one amplicon consistently drops out in a subset of samples. Sequence inspection shows a variant under the primer binding site, which weakens pairing and reduces amplification, so the team redesigns the primer rather than reporting the resulting coverage gap as a deletion.
common_misunderstanding: Base pair and base are often used as if interchangeable. A read length of one hundred and fifty bases is not one hundred and fifty base pairs of information unless the molecule is double-stranded, and the distinction matters in reporting. A second error is assuming pairing is perfectly specific; mismatched duplexes form readily under permissive conditions, which is how off-target amplification arises.

plain_definition: A codon is a group of three consecutive bases in a messenger RNA that specifies one amino acid during protein synthesis, or signals that synthesis should stop. Reading a coding sequence three bases at a time gives the order of amino acids in the protein. There are sixty-four possible codons, and most amino acids are specified by more than one of them.
technical_explanation: Codons are read sequentially by the ribosome within a reading frame established at the initiation codon, usually AUG, which also specifies methionine. Sixty-one codons specify amino acids and three act as termination signals. The code is degenerate: synonymous codons encode the same amino acid, commonly differing at the third position, which is why many substitutions at that position do not change the protein sequence. Synonymous changes are nonetheless not always neutral, since codon usage influences translation speed, messenger RNA stability and splicing regulatory elements, and a synonymous variant can disrupt a splice site. Variant nomenclature distinguishes changes described at the complementary DNA level from their predicted protein consequence, and classification frameworks treat predicted protein effect as one line of evidence among several rather than as proof of pathogenicity. Codon usage also differs between organisms, which matters when expressing a human gene in bacteria or designing synthetic constructs. A practical limitation is that predicting consequence from codon change alone ignores context such as transcript choice and tissue-specific splicing.
practical_example: A bioinformatician annotating a variant sees a synonymous change at the third position of a codon and would normally deprioritise it. Because the position lies at the edge of an exon, the analyst checks splice predictions, which suggest the change weakens the donor site, and the variant is kept for further assessment rather than filtered out.
common_misunderstanding: It is widely assumed that synonymous codon changes are harmless and that a change of amino acid is harmful. Neither holds reliably: some synonymous changes disrupt splicing or translation, while many amino acid substitutions are tolerated. Predicted protein consequence is evidence to be weighed, not a classification in itself.

plain_definition: The genetic code is the set of rules by which cells translate the sequence of bases in a messenger RNA into the sequence of amino acids in a protein. Bases are read in groups of three, and each group corresponds to one amino acid or to a stop signal. The same code is used by almost all living things, with a few known exceptions.
technical_explanation: The standard genetic code maps sixty-four triplets onto twenty amino acids plus termination. Its near-universality is strong evidence of common ancestry and is what allows a gene from one organism to be expressed in another. Exceptions exist: mitochondria in several lineages, including human mitochondria, reassign particular codons, and some ciliates and bacteria use alternative assignments, so translating a mitochondrial sequence with the standard table produces wrong protein predictions. The code is also structured rather than arbitrary, since codons differing at the third position often specify the same or chemically similar amino acids, which buffers the effect of many substitutions. Selenocysteine and pyrrolysine are incorporated at particular stop codons through specialised context-dependent mechanisms. In practice, software that translates nucleotide sequence requires the correct translation table and the correct reading frame, and specifying neither is a common source of nonsense output. The code says nothing about whether a sequence is actually transcribed or translated in a given cell.
practical_example: An analyst translating a mitochondrial gene with default software settings obtains a protein riddled with premature stops. Switching to the vertebrate mitochondrial translation table resolves the apparent nonsense, illustrating why the translation table is recorded explicitly in pipelines rather than left at whichever default a tool happens to apply.
common_misunderstanding: People often describe the genetic code as universal without qualification. Several translation tables exist, and mitochondrial and some microbial sequences follow different assignments. A second misunderstanding treats the genetic code as the whole of genetic information; it governs only the protein-coding step and says nothing about regulation, splicing or non-coding RNA function.

plain_definition: Transcription is the process by which a cell copies a stretch of DNA into RNA. An enzyme called RNA polymerase binds near the start of a gene, unwinds the two DNA strands and builds an RNA molecule that matches one of them. The resulting RNA may carry instructions for a protein or may itself do a job in the cell.
technical_explanation: Transcription begins when RNA polymerase and associated factors assemble at a promoter, aided in eukaryotes by distal enhancers brought into proximity by chromatin folding. The enzyme synthesises RNA in the five-prime to three-prime direction using the template strand, so the transcript matches the coding strand with uracil replacing thymine. Eukaryotic transcripts are processed co-transcriptionally: a cap is added at the five-prime end, introns are removed by the spliceosome and a polyadenylated tail is added after cleavage. Regulation operates at initiation, pausing and elongation, and is shaped by transcription factor availability, chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation at regulatory regions. Measuring transcription is not the same as measuring steady-state RNA: standard RNA sequencing quantifies abundance, which reflects both synthesis and degradation, so methods such as metabolic labelling are needed to separate the two. A further limitation is that short-read data infer transcript structure statistically, and isoform-level estimates are less certain than gene-level ones, particularly for genes with many overlapping isoforms.
practical_example: A research group comparing treated and untreated cells finds a gene with higher transcript abundance after treatment. Because abundance reflects both synthesis and decay, they cannot conclude that transcription increased, and they add an experiment that labels newly made RNA before making that claim in the manuscript.
common_misunderstanding: Transcription and translation are frequently swapped in casual use. Transcription makes RNA from DNA; translation makes protein from RNA. A further error is to assume a transcribed region must be functional, since pervasive low-level transcription occurs across much of the genome and detecting a transcript is not evidence that it does anything.

plain_definition: Translation is the process by which a cell builds a protein using the instructions carried in a messenger RNA. Ribosomes move along the messenger RNA reading its bases three at a time, and transfer RNA molecules deliver the matching amino acids. The amino acids are joined into a chain that folds into a working protein. Translation stops at a stop signal.
technical_explanation: Translation proceeds through initiation, elongation and termination. In eukaryotes the small ribosomal subunit is recruited to the capped five-prime end and scans to an initiation codon in a favourable sequence context, after which the large subunit joins and elongation begins. Aminoacyl transfer RNAs deliver amino acids matched to each codon, peptide bonds form in the ribosomal peptidyl transferase centre, and release factors act at stop codons. Rates of elongation vary with codon usage and transfer RNA availability, influencing co-translational folding. Quality control pathways, notably nonsense-mediated decay, degrade transcripts carrying premature termination codons, which is why a stop-gain variant often reduces protein quantity rather than producing a truncated product, though position within the transcript determines whether decay is triggered. Clinically this distinction matters, since loss-of-function interpretation depends on whether the mechanism of disease is haploinsufficiency. A limitation of transcript-level data is that it does not report translation, and ribosome profiling or proteomics is required to measure what is actually synthesised.
practical_example: A variant assessment team encounters a stop-gain variant in the final exon of a gene. Because premature termination there is unlikely to trigger nonsense-mediated decay, a truncated protein may be produced, so the team weighs loss-of-function evidence more cautiously than it would for an equivalent variant in an early exon.
common_misunderstanding: A common assumption is that any premature stop codon abolishes the protein. The cellular consequence depends on position and on whether the transcript is degraded, and some truncated proteins retain or gain activity. Assuming that abundant messenger RNA implies abundant protein is a related error, since translation efficiency and protein turnover vary considerably.

plain_definition: A promoter is a stretch of DNA just before a gene where the machinery that makes RNA first assembles. It acts as a starting signal, setting where transcription begins and influencing how often it happens. Promoters contain short sequence patterns recognised by proteins, and their activity can differ between tissues and between conditions within the same organism.
technical_explanation: A promoter is the regulatory region surrounding a transcription start site at which general transcription factors and RNA polymerase assemble. Core promoter elements provide positioning signals, while proximal and distal elements, including enhancers acting over long distances through chromatin looping, set the level of transcription. Many human promoters lie in CpG islands that are typically unmethylated when the associated gene is active, and aberrant promoter methylation is a recognised mechanism of gene silencing, including silencing of tumour suppressor genes in cancer. Promoter usage is not fixed per gene: alternative promoters generate transcripts with different first exons and sometimes different protein products or tissue distributions. Experimentally, promoter activity is assessed by reporter assays, accessibility assays and start-site mapping, each measuring a different proxy. A limitation for variant interpretation is that non-coding promoter variants are difficult to classify, because evidence frameworks were built around coding consequence and functional data for individual regulatory positions are usually absent.
practical_example: An analyst investigating an unsolved case finds no coding variant but notes a rare change in the promoter of a strong candidate gene. Without functional data or recurrent observations in similarly affected individuals, the finding remains of uncertain significance, and the laboratory records it as a research observation rather than a diagnostic result.
common_misunderstanding: Promoters are often imagined as simple on switches sitting immediately before every gene. Transcriptional control is distributed across promoters, enhancers, insulators and chromatin state, many genes have several promoters, and promoter activity varies by cell type. A variant in a promoter is therefore not automatically consequential, nor automatically harmless.

plain_definition: An exon is a part of a gene that is kept in the finished RNA molecule after the gene has been copied and edited. Most human genes are split into several exons separated by sequences that are removed. Exons may contain the instructions for part of a protein, or they may carry untranslated sequence at either end of the RNA.
technical_explanation: Exons are the segments retained in a mature transcript after splicing. They include coding sequence and the untranslated regions at the five-prime and three-prime ends, so exon and coding sequence are not synonymous. Exon boundaries are defined by splice donor and acceptor sites, and exon numbering is transcript-specific, which is why clinical reports quote a transcript identifier alongside any exon reference. Exome sequencing targets exonic sequence with capture probes, concentrating effort on the small fraction of the genome where most currently interpretable disease-associated variants lie, but capture is uneven: regions of extreme base composition, recent duplications and some first exons are covered poorly, and non-coding regulatory variants are missed entirely by design. Alternative splicing means that an exon included in one transcript may be skipped in another, so describing a variant as exonic is incomplete without naming the transcript. Exon-level analysis of RNA sequencing data can reveal splicing changes that gene-level summaries conceal.
practical_example: A diagnostic laboratory reports a variant in exon eleven of a gene. A colleague comparing it with an older publication that numbered exons according to a different transcript finds the positions appear to disagree, and the discrepancy resolves once both are mapped to the same reference transcript.
common_misunderstanding: Exons are often equated with protein-coding sequence. Untranslated regions are exonic too, and they carry elements that affect transcript stability and translation. A second misunderstanding is that exome sequencing covers all exons; capture efficiency varies, and a region reported as negative may simply have been sequenced too shallowly to call.

plain_definition: An intron is a section of a gene that is copied into the initial RNA molecule but then cut out before the RNA is used. The remaining pieces, called exons, are joined together. Introns are common in the genes of plants, animals and fungi, and although they are removed, sequences within and around them help control how the RNA is assembled.
technical_explanation: Introns are removed from precursor messenger RNA by the spliceosome, which recognises the donor site at the intron's five-prime end, a branch point, a polypyrimidine tract and the acceptor site at the three-prime end. Introns are typically far longer than the exons they separate and contain regulatory elements, small nucleolar and microRNA genes, and sequences that influence splice-site choice. RNA sequencing of a relevant tissue can demonstrate aberrant splicing directly, though the causal tissue is often inaccessible, which limits the approach. Intron retention also occurs physiologically and is a recognised regulatory mechanism rather than always an error.

plain_definition: RNA splicing is the editing step in which a cell removes the intervening sections of a freshly made RNA molecule and joins the remaining pieces together. This produces a continuous sequence ready to be read for protein synthesis. Many genes can be spliced in more than one way, so a single gene can give rise to several different RNA molecules and proteins.
technical_explanation: Splicing is catalysed by the spliceosome, a complex of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins and associated proteins that recognises donor and acceptor sites, the branch point and auxiliary splicing enhancer and silencer elements located in both exons and introns. Variants that disrupt canonical splice dinucleotides are strong candidates for loss of function, while variants further from the junction require prediction tools and, ideally, functional confirmation. Splicing is measured from RNA sequencing by quantifying junction-spanning reads and by isoform-level inference, but short reads make full-length isoform reconstruction uncertain, and long-read sequencing resolves this more directly. Interpretation depends on tissue: a splicing effect present in neurons may be absent in blood, so a negative result in an accessible tissue does not exclude an effect elsewhere.

plain_definition: Messenger RNA, usually abbreviated to mRNA, is the type of RNA that carries the instructions from a gene to the machinery that makes proteins. It is produced by copying a gene, edited to remove intervening sections, and then read three bases at a time to assemble a protein. The amount of a given messenger RNA in a cell reflects how active that gene currently is.
technical_explanation: Mature eukaryotic messenger RNA carries a seven-methylguanosine cap, a spliced coding sequence flanked by untranslated regions, and a polyadenylated tail. These features support export from the nucleus, ribosome recruitment and transcript stability, and they are also what sequencing protocols exploit, since poly-A selection enriches messenger RNA while ribosomal depletion retains non-polyadenylated species and degraded material. Transcript abundance is quantified from RNA sequencing after normalisation for library size and composition, and differential expression testing uses count-based models that account for overdispersion. Interpretation requires care: abundance depends on both synthesis and decay, correlates only moderately with protein levels, and is sensitive to sample handling, since RNA degrades quickly without stabilisation. Synthetic messenger RNA is also used therapeutically, as in messenger RNA vaccines, where modified nucleosides and lipid formulation address instability and innate immune activation. Note that in other contexts mRNA is occasionally used loosely for any coding transcript, including unspliced precursors, so precision in writing is worthwhile.

common_misunderstanding: Messenger RNA is often treated as a direct readout of protein level. Transcript and protein abundance correlate imperfectly because translation and degradation are regulated separately. A second misunderstanding is that messenger RNA vaccines alter a person's DNA; the molecule is transient, acts in the cytoplasm and has no mechanism for integrating into the genome.

plain_definition: An open reading frame is a stretch of sequence that could be read as a continuous set of three-letter codons without hitting a stop signal. Because sequence can be read in several frames and on either strand, software looks for such stretches when predicting where protein-coding genes might lie. An open reading frame is a candidate for coding, not proof of it.
technical_explanation: An open reading frame is a run of codons bounded by an initiation codon and the first in-frame termination codon, identified in one of six possible frames across the two strands. Open reading frame finding is a basic step in prokaryotic gene prediction, where genes are typically uninterrupted and gene density is high, and it is far less sufficient in eukaryotes because introns break coding sequence across exons. Length thresholds reduce spurious predictions, since short open reading frames occur frequently by chance in any sequence, but thresholds also discard genuine short coding sequences, a class increasingly recognised as functional. Supporting evidence from homology, transcript data, ribosome profiling and proteomics is therefore used to promote a predicted open reading frame to an annotated gene. In clinical variant work the concept appears when assessing frameshifts, since an insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three shifts the frame and usually introduces a premature stop. Note that the abbreviation ORF is also used informally for the predicted protein product itself.

Many short predictions lack any database match or transcript support, so the annotation pipeline flags them as hypothetical rather than asserting function, and the team reports only well-supported genes in the manuscript.

It is a sequence pattern that may or may not be transcribed and translated, and in eukaryotes genuine coding sequence is usually split across exons so that no single genomic open reading frame spans the gene. plain_definition: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence compared with what was there before. Mutations arise from errors during DNA copying, from chemical damage, or from exposure to agents such as radiation. They may be inherited from a parent or acquired during a person's lifetime. Most have no noticeable effect, some are harmful, and a few are advantageous.
technical_explanation: Mutation denotes the process or event by which sequence changes, and historically the word was also used for the resulting sequence difference. Current clinical practice prefers variant for the observed difference, with pathogenicity stated separately, because mutation carries an unintended implication of harm and because the same change may be common and benign in some populations. Mutations are classified by mechanism and scale: substitutions, small insertions and deletions, structural rearrangements and copy-number changes. Germline mutations occur in the gametes or early embryo and can be transmitted; somatic mutations arise in body cells and contribute to cancer and to mosaicism without being passed to offspring. Mutation rates vary with sequence context, replication timing, parental age and exposure, and characteristic patterns of somatic change form mutational signatures that can indicate underlying processes such as ultraviolet damage or defective mismatch repair. A key limitation is that detecting a sequence change says nothing by itself about consequence, which requires separate evidence.

Changes shared with blood are germline and are handled under consent provisions for inherited findings, while tumour-only changes are somatic, and conflating the two would misdirect both treatment discussion and family follow-up.
common_misunderstanding: Mutation is widely assumed to mean something harmful or abnormal. Most sequence changes are neutral, variation between individuals is ordinary, and harm depends on the specific change and context. The term also blurs an important distinction: a change in a tumour is not inherited, whereas a germline change may be, and the implications for relatives differ entirely.

plain_definition: A variant is a difference between the DNA sequence observed in a sample and the sequence of the reference used for comparison. Variants are ordinary: every person carries millions of them. A variant is simply a difference, and saying that one exists tells you nothing about whether it affects health. That judgement requires separate evidence and a formal classification process.
technical_explanation: Variant is the preferred neutral term for an observed sequence difference, replacing earlier usage in which mutation implied harm and polymorphism implied benignity by frequency alone. Variants are described against a named reference assembly and transcript using standard nomenclature, and they span classes from single-nucleotide changes and small insertions or deletions to structural and copy-number events. Clinical classification under consensus frameworks weighs population frequency, computational prediction, functional data, segregation in families and case-control evidence to place a variant into categories from benign to pathogenic, with uncertain significance used when evidence is insufficient. Classifications are provisional and are revised as evidence accumulates, so laboratories operate reinterpretation policies. Frequency data are population-specific, and because reference datasets under-represent many populations, variants common in those groups have historically been over-called as candidate disease variants. Detection also varies by class and technology: structural and repeat-expansion variants are poorly captured by standard short-read pipelines, so absence of a reported variant is not evidence that none exists.

Larger and more diverse population datasets now show it at appreciable frequency in an ancestry group that was barely represented when the original assessment was made, and the classification is revised accordingly and reissued.
common_misunderstanding: The word variant is often read as a synonym for something wrong. A variant is a difference from a reference sequence, and the reference is a convention rather than a standard of health. It is equally mistaken to assume a variant classification is permanent; classifications reflect current evidence and are expected to change.

plain_definition: A single-nucleotide variant, abbreviated to SNV, is a change of one DNA letter at one position compared with a reference sequence. It is the most common kind of difference between individuals and also a frequent change acquired by cells over time. Whether a single-nucleotide variant matters depends on where it falls and what it does, not on its size.
technical_explanation: A single-nucleotide variant is a substitution at one position, distinguished from a single-nucleotide polymorphism chiefly by convention: polymorphism historically implied a frequency above about one per cent in a population, while variant makes no claim about frequency and is preferred in clinical reporting. Calling single-nucleotide variants from short reads involves alignment, local realignment or assembly, and a probabilistic model of base quality and read support, with filters tuned to balance sensitivity against false positives. Germline calling assumes expected allele fractions near one half or one, whereas somatic calling must detect low fractions in impure, subclonal tumour samples and therefore uses matched normal samples and error models designed for low-frequency signal. Consequences range from synonymous changes to missense, nonsense and splice-affecting changes, and non-coding substitutions may alter regulatory elements. Context-specific artefacts, including oxidative damage introduced during library preparation and deamination in formalin-fixed material, produce characteristic false substitutions, which is why strand bias and mutational context are inspected before reporting.

Single-base changes include some of the best characterised disease-associated variants, and conversely most are without consequence. Equating single-nucleotide variant with single-nucleotide polymorphism is a second error, since the latter carries an implication about population frequency.

plain_definition: An insertion or deletion, often shortened to indel, is a variant in which extra DNA letters are added or existing letters are removed compared with a reference sequence. Indels range from a single letter to many. Within protein-coding sequence, an indel whose length is not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame and usually disrupts the protein that follows.
technical_explanation: Indels are the second most common class of small variant after substitutions. In coding sequence, in-frame indels add or remove whole codons, whereas frameshifting indels change every downstream codon and typically introduce a premature termination codon, with consequences that depend on whether nonsense-mediated decay is triggered. Detection is harder than for substitutions: reads must be aligned across the gap, and short reads in repetitive or homopolymeric sequence frequently produce ambiguous placements, so haplotype-based callers that locally reassemble reads outperform simple position-based approaches. Representation is also ambiguous, since the same indel can be written at different positions within a repeat, and left-alignment and normalisation are required before variant sets can be compared or merged. Homopolymer-length errors are a known weakness of some sequencing chemistries, including early nanopore data, which has improved substantially but still warrants care. Larger insertions and deletions grade into structural variants, with no universally agreed size boundary, so pipelines state their own thresholds.

Normalising both call sets to a common left-aligned representation shows that the two laboratories had reported the identical indel in different but equivalent notation, and the apparent discrepancy disappears without any re-sequencing.

A single-base insertion in coding sequence can abolish a protein, while a large in-frame deletion may be tolerated, so length alone predicts little. plain_definition: Dominant inheritance describes a pattern in which a single altered copy of a gene is enough to produce a trait or condition, even though the other copy is unchanged. A person with such a variant has, on average, a one in two chance of passing it to each child. Dominant conditions often appear in several generations of a family.
technical_explanation: Dominance is a property of the relationship between a variant and a phenotype, not an intrinsic property of a gene. Mechanisms include haploinsufficiency, where half the normal gene product is insufficient, and dominant-negative or gain-of-function effects, where the altered product interferes with or exceeds normal activity. Autosomal dominant pedigrees typically show affected individuals in successive generations with male-to-male transmission possible, but the pattern is frequently obscured by incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, de novo occurrence in the first affected person, mosaicism in a parent, and small family size. Age-dependent penetrance means an unaffected older relative does not exclude a variant. Quantitative traits rarely behave in a simply dominant manner, and most common conditions are polygenic rather than following Mendelian patterns. Recurrence figures quoted in counselling describe transmission of the variant, which is distinct from the probability of developing the condition when penetrance is incomplete; the two are often conflated in general writing.

Testing shows one parent carries the same variant without features of the condition, consistent with reduced penetrance, so the family discussion covers variable outcomes rather than treating the parent's result as excluding inheritance.
common_misunderstanding: Dominant is often understood to mean stronger or more harmful. It describes only whether one altered copy suffices to produce the phenotype under study. It is also wrong to assume everyone carrying a dominant disease-associated variant will be affected: penetrance is frequently incomplete and severity varies widely within one family.

plain_definition: Recessive inheritance describes a pattern in which both copies of a gene must be altered before a trait or condition appears. Someone with one altered copy and one unaltered copy is usually unaffected and is described as a carrier. When both parents are carriers, each child has about a one in four chance of inheriting both altered copies.
technical_explanation: In autosomal recessive conditions, affected individuals carry variants on both copies of a gene, either the same variant twice or two different variants, one on each parental chromosome. Establishing that two variants lie in trans, meaning on opposite copies, is essential, and parental testing or read-based phasing provides this; two variants in cis on the same copy leave an intact gene and do not explain a recessive condition. Carrier frequencies differ between populations because of demographic history including founder effects and consanguinity, so carrier screening panels designed for one population perform differently elsewhere, and panels assembled largely from European data under-detect in other groups. Carriers are generally unaffected but may show measurable biochemical differences, and for some conditions, such as sickle cell trait, the carrier state has recognised physiological consequences under particular circumstances. Pedigrees may show affected siblings without affected parents, and in small families the pattern can be indistinguishable from a sporadic occurrence.
practical_example: A genetics service assessing a child with an inherited metabolic condition finds two variants in the relevant gene. Parental samples show one variant in each parent, confirming they lie on opposite chromosome copies, which supports the diagnosis in a way that the child's result alone could not.
common_misunderstanding: Carriers are often assumed to be at risk of developing the condition themselves. For most recessive conditions a single altered copy does not cause disease, although it is relevant to reproductive planning. A further misunderstanding is that recessive conditions are rare everywhere; carrier frequencies vary between populations, and some are common in particular communities.

plain_definition: X-linked inheritance describes patterns produced by genes on the X chromosome. Because people with one X chromosome have only a single copy of those genes, an altered copy is expressed directly, whereas people with two X chromosomes have a second copy that may compensate. This produces family patterns that differ from those of genes on the other chromosomes.
technical_explanation: Genes on the X chromosome are present in one copy in individuals with an XY karyotype, a hemizygous state in which a single altered copy is fully expressed. In individuals with two X chromosomes, random X inactivation silences one X in each cell, so the proportion of cells expressing the altered copy varies, which explains why carriers of X-linked recessive conditions may show mild or patchy features and why skewed inactivation can produce more substantial involvement. X-linked dominant conditions affect both sexes, sometimes with male lethality, and affected fathers transmit the variant to all daughters and no sons. Pseudoautosomal regions at the ends of the X and Y chromosomes recombine and behave autosomally. Analytically, X-chromosome data require ploidy-aware variant calling and sex-aware association analysis, and inferred chromosomal sex from sequencing data may differ from recorded sex, which must be handled with care and without assumptions about gender identity.

Rather than assuming an error in the record, the team treats the finding as a quality control flag, checks for sample mix-up and for sex-chromosome variation, and follows the study's agreed procedure.
common_misunderstanding: X-linked recessive conditions are often described as affecting only males and never carriers. Carriers can show features because X inactivation is random and sometimes skewed. plain_definition: Mendelian inheritance describes traits and conditions determined largely by variants in a single gene, passed on in predictable patterns first described by Gregor Mendel. The main patterns are dominant, recessive and those linked to the X chromosome. Many rare conditions follow these patterns, while most common traits and diseases involve many genes together with environmental influences.
technical_explanation: Mendelian conditions arise from variants in a single gene with a large effect on phenotype, and their pedigrees follow recognisable segregation patterns. They are individually rare but collectively substantial, and sequencing has greatly expanded the catalogue of genes implicated. Diagnostic analysis proceeds by filtering variants on rarity in population databases, predicted consequence, inheritance model and gene-phenotype match, then weighing evidence under consensus classification frameworks. Diagnostic yield remains well short of complete, reflecting non-coding causes, structural and repeat variants missed by standard assays, genes not yet linked to disease, and phenotypes that are not in fact monogenic. Mendelian expectation is complicated by incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, imprinting, mosaicism, de novo variation and digenic contributions, and by polygenic background that modifies severity even in single-gene conditions. Reference data under-representing many populations reduce the reliability of rarity filters outside well-sampled groups, which is a recognised source of both missed diagnoses and over-calling.

One candidate is rare in the main reference datasets but turns out to be relatively common in a population poorly represented there, so the team seeks additional ancestry-matched frequency data before drawing conclusions.
common_misunderstanding: Mendelian is often taken to mean that one gene straightforwardly determines one outcome. Even in single-gene conditions, severity and age of onset vary, and some carriers remain unaffected. The converse error is to expect Mendelian patterns for common diseases, where risk is distributed across many variants of small effect plus environment.

plain_definition: Meiosis is the specialised form of cell division that produces eggs and sperm. It halves the number of chromosomes so that each gamete carries one copy of each chromosome instead of two. When egg and sperm combine, the full number is restored. Meiosis also shuffles the genetic material inherited from each parent, so siblings are genetically different.
technical_explanation: Meiosis consists of one round of DNA replication followed by two divisions. In prophase of the first division, homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments by recombination at crossover sites, producing chromatids that combine maternal and paternal sequence. Independent assortment of homologues at the first division and separation of sister chromatids at the second generate haploid cells whose combinations are effectively unique. Errors in segregation produce gametes with extra or missing chromosomes, the basis of aneuploidy, and the risk of certain segregation errors increases with maternal age. Recombination is not uniform along chromosomes: rates concentrate in hotspots, and the resulting pattern of linkage disequilibrium is what makes genome-wide association and imputation possible. Meiotic recombination also occasionally produces structural rearrangements through non-allelic homologous recombination between repeated sequences, a recognised mechanism for recurrent copy-number variants. Understanding meiosis underpins the interpretation of inheritance patterns and of population genetic structure.

The most common origin of such an imbalance is a segregation error during the formation of a gamete, and explaining this origin helps a counselling team describe why the finding usually does not indicate anything the parents did or could have prevented.
common_misunderstanding: Meiosis is often confused with mitosis. Mitosis produces two genetically identical cells for growth and repair, whereas meiosis produces four genetically distinct haploid cells for reproduction. Another misconception is that a chromosome passed on is a single parental chromosome; recombination means most transmitted chromosomes are mosaics of both grandparental copies.

plain_definition: Genetic recombination is the exchange of segments of DNA between two chromosomes or DNA molecules. In people it happens mainly during the formation of eggs and sperm, when matching chromosomes swap sections. The result is that the chromosome a child inherits is a mixture of the two copies carried by that parent, so each child receives a different combination.
technical_explanation: In meiosis, programmed double-strand breaks are repaired using the homologous chromosome as a template, producing crossovers that exchange segments, alongside non-crossover gene conversion events that transfer short tracts. Crossovers are not uniformly distributed; in many species they cluster in hotspots, and rates differ between the sexes and among individuals. The resulting shuffling breaks down associations between nearby variants over generations, generating the pattern of linkage disequilibrium that underpins tagging in genotyping arrays, haplotype phasing and imputation. Recombination between repeated sequences that are not true alleles, termed non-allelic homologous recombination, can delete, duplicate or invert intervening segments and explains several recurrent copy-number syndromes. In microorganisms, recombination also occurs through horizontal transfer, conjugation and phage-mediated exchange, which complicates phylogenetic inference because a single tree may not describe the whole genome. Analysts therefore test for recombination before interpreting pathogen trees, as unrecognised recombination can distort branch lengths and inflate apparent evolutionary rates.

Several dense clusters of differences are attributed to imported sequence rather than to point change, and masking those regions substantially alters the inferred relationships between isolates and the conclusions drawn about transmission.

Every meiosis produces crossovers on most chromosomes, and over generations the effect is pervasive. In microbial genomics a different error is to assume a single tree describes the genome; recombination means different regions can have different histories.

plain_definition: A karyotype is the complete set of chromosomes in a cell, and also the laboratory image in which those chromosomes are arranged in order by size and banding pattern. Examining a karyotype shows how many chromosomes are present and whether any large pieces are missing, duplicated or rearranged. It is one of the oldest techniques in genetics and remains useful.
technical_explanation: Conventional karyotyping requires dividing cells, which are arrested in metaphase, spread, stained to produce reproducible banding and then examined microscopically. Results are described in standardised cytogenetic nomenclature stating chromosome number, sex chromosome constitution and any structural findings. Resolution is limited to imbalances of roughly five to ten megabases, so chromosomal microarray and sequencing-based copy-number analysis are used when smaller imbalances are suspected. Karyotyping retains advantages those methods lack: it detects balanced translocations and inversions, which leave copy number unchanged, and it reveals mosaicism and marker chromosomes directly. It also requires viable, culturable cells, which limits its use on some sample types and lengthens turnaround compared with molecular methods. In haemato-oncology, karyotyping of bone marrow remains part of standard characterisation because recurrent structural rearrangements carry prognostic meaning, often complemented by fluorescence in situ hybridisation for specific targets.

The karyotype reveals a balanced rearrangement that a copy-number array would not have detected, and this structural finding becomes part of the disease classification discussed at the multidisciplinary meeting.

Sequencing and arrays outperform it for small imbalances but can miss balanced rearrangements and give a less direct view of mosaicism. The opposite error is to treat a normal karyotype as excluding a genetic cause, when its resolution is measured in megabases.

plain_definition: Aneuploidy means having a number of chromosomes that differs from the usual complement for that organism, such as one extra copy or one missing copy. In humans it usually arises when chromosomes fail to separate correctly during the formation of eggs or sperm. Aneuploidy is also very common in cancer cells, where whole chromosomes are frequently gained or lost.
technical_explanation: Aneuploidy results from non-disjunction during meiosis or mitosis, or from anaphase lag, and produces gain or loss of whole chromosomes rather than the segmental imbalances described as copy-number variants. Most autosomal aneuploidies are not compatible with continued development, and those that are, together with sex-chromosome aneuploidies, produce varied phenotypes influenced by mosaicism and by which chromosome is involved. Maternal age is an established risk factor for certain meiotic segregation errors. In tumours, aneuploidy is pervasive and arises from chromosomal instability, contributing to clonal diversity and treatment resistance. Detection methods differ in what they can see: karyotyping visualises whole-chromosome change directly, arrays and sequencing infer it from coverage or allele ratios, and cell-free DNA screening in pregnancy estimates chromosomal proportions from a maternal blood sample. The last is a screening approach, not a diagnostic one, and results require confirmatory testing because placental mosaicism and other factors can produce discordant findings.

Recording this chromosome-scale pattern alongside the point variants gives a fuller description of the tumour genome than a list of substitutions alone would provide.

It covers any departure from the usual chromosome number, including losses, sex-chromosome changes and the widespread gains and losses seen in tumours. A separate error is treating a screening result based on cell-free DNA as diagnostic, when it estimates risk and requires confirmation.

plain_definition: Epigenetics is the study of changes that affect how genes are used without altering the underlying DNA sequence. These include chemical marks added to DNA or to the proteins that package it, which influence whether a gene is switched on or off. Such marks differ between tissues and can change over time and with environment, and some persist through cell division.
technical_explanation: Epigenetic mechanisms include DNA methylation, covalent histone modification, chromatin remodelling, non-coding RNA activity and higher-order genome organisation. Together they establish and maintain cell-type-specific gene expression patterns from a single genome, which is why liver and neuron differ despite identical sequence. Epigenetic marks are mitotically heritable in somatic lineages; transmission across generations in humans is largely reset during gametogenesis and early development and remains contested, with imprinted loci as the clearest exception. Measurement techniques target specific layers: bisulphite-based sequencing and arrays for methylation, chromatin immunoprecipitation for histone marks, accessibility assays for open chromatin. Interpretation is constrained by tissue specificity, since blood-derived measurements may not reflect the tissue of interest, and by cell composition, because a mixed sample yields an average that can shift simply because the cell mixture changed. Causality is also hard to establish: an epigenetic difference associated with a disease may be a consequence of it rather than a driver.

Because blood cell proportions also differ between the groups, the analysts adjust for estimated cell composition, and a large part of the apparent signal resolves, illustrating why composition is modelled rather than ignored.

Somatic epigenetic change is well established, but robust evidence for transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans is limited, since most marks are reset in the germ line. A further error is reading an epigenetic association as a cause when it may be a downstream consequence.

plain_definition: DNA methylation is the addition of a small chemical group to a DNA base, most often a cytosine followed by a guanine. The sequence itself is unchanged, but the mark influences whether nearby genes are switched on. Patterns of methylation differ between tissues, are copied when cells divide, and change during development, with age and in disease.

plain_definition: Gene expression is the process by which the information in a gene is used to make a product, usually a protein. It is also the term for how much of that product a cell makes. plain_definition: Minor allele frequency, or MAF, is how often the less common of two versions of a DNA position is seen in a group of people. plain_definition: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes the simple relationship expected between how often each allele occurs and how often each genotype occurs, in a large population that mates at random and in which nothing is disturbing the alleles. plain_definition: Population structure means that the people in a dataset are not one randomly mixing group: allele frequencies differ systematically between subgroups because of geography, history, migration and patterns of partnership. plain_definition: Genetic drift is the change in how common an allele is from one generation to the next, caused simply by chance in who reproduces and which copies are passed on. plain_definition: Natural selection is the process by which inherited differences that affect survival or reproduction become more or less common across generations. plain_definition: A founder effect occurs when a small group separates from a larger population and establishes a new one. plain_definition: A genome-wide association study, or GWAS, tests hundreds of thousands to millions of positions across the genome to see whether any version of a position occurs more often in people with a trait than in people without it. technical_explanation: A polygenic score is typically a weighted sum of allele counts, with weights taken from GWAS summary statistics and adjusted for linkage disequilibrium by clumping and thresholding or by Bayesian shrinkage. Performance is reported as variance explained, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, or odds ratio per standard deviation, always relative to the distribution in a specified population. The raw score is dimensionless and interpretable only after standardisation against that reference. Portability is the central problem: scores derived in European-ancestry cohorts lose accuracy when applied to people of other ancestries, because tagging variants sit in different linkage disequilibrium with causal variants, allele frequencies differ, and effect estimates may not transfer. Deploying such scores without ancestry-appropriate derivation and validation risks widening rather than narrowing health inequalities. plain_definition: Heritability is the share of the differences between people in a trait, within a particular population and set of environments, that can be attributed to differences in their genes. It is a property of a group rather than of an individual, and it changes when the population or the environment changes. A high value does not mean a trait is fixed or beyond modification.
technical_explanation: Narrow-sense heritability is the proportion of phenotypic variance explained by additive genetic variance; broad-sense heritability also includes dominance and interaction effects. Classical estimates come from twin and family designs that partition observed resemblance, while SNP-based heritability is estimated among unrelated individuals using genomic relationship matrices, or from GWAS summary statistics by LD score regression. These estimators answer related but distinct questions, and SNP-based values are generally lower than twin-based ones, the so-called missing heritability gap, because common genotyped variants do not capture rare variation or every source of familial resemblance. Every estimate is conditional on the population sampled and the range of environments present: narrow the environmental variation and heritability rises even though the underlying biology is unchanged. Estimates can also be inflated by shared environment, assortative mating and residual population structure. Crucially, heritability places no limit on how much an environmental intervention can shift a trait, and heritability within groups says nothing about the causes of differences between groups.

It is a statement about variance between people in a sampled population, not a split within any individual. plain_definition: Genotype imputation fills in positions that were not directly measured, by comparing the positions that were measured against a reference panel of people whose genomes are known in detail. Because nearby variants travel together on shared stretches of chromosome, matching those stretches lets software predict the missing genotypes, together with a confidence value for each prediction.
technical_explanation: Imputation takes sparse genotypes, usually from an array, phases them into haplotypes, and matches those haplotypes against a dense reference panel using hidden Markov models, returning posterior genotype probabilities or dosages plus a quality metric such as an info or r-squared score. It raises effective marker density by one to two orders of magnitude, enabling meta-analysis across studies genotyped on different arrays and improving fine-mapping resolution. Accuracy depends on reference panel size, on how closely panel haplotypes resemble those in the target sample, and on allele frequency, since rare variants impute far less reliably than common ones. Panels built predominantly from European-ancestry samples impute African and admixed genomes poorly, which is a practical driver for expanding diverse and multi-ancestry panels. They are probabilistic predictions conditional on a reference panel, and their reliability varies by variant, by allele frequency and by how well the panel represents the sample. plain_definition: A reference genome is an agreed, assembled DNA sequence used as a shared coordinate system, so that laboratories everywhere can describe positions and variants in the same way. The current human reference is a mosaic built from a small number of donors. It is a convenient yardstick rather than a model of a healthy or typical person, and it does not contain all human variation.

Successive builds, including GRCh37, GRCh38 and the telomere-to-telomere assembly that resolved previously missing regions such as centromeric satellite arrays and acrocentric short arms, use different coordinates, so results must always be reported with their build and lifted over carefully when datasets are combined. The assembly is a haploid consensus derived from several donors, with alternate loci supplied for highly polymorphic regions such as the major histocompatibility complex. This design creates reference bias: reads carrying non-reference alleles align less readily, so variation is under-called wherever a sample's true sequence diverges from the reference, an effect distributed unevenly across populations because the donor panel was not globally representative. It is a composite coordinate framework, it carries rare and minor alleles at many sites, and it under-represents variation found in populations absent from the original donor set. Differing from the reference means being different, not being abnormal.
