plain_definition: The reproduction number is the average number of new infections caused by one infected person. The basic reproduction number, written R0, applies to a fully susceptible population, while the effective reproduction number applies to the population as it actually is, with immunity and control measures in place. A value above one means the epidemic is growing.
technical_explanation: The basic reproduction number is a theoretical quantity for a wholly susceptible, homogeneously mixing population, determined by transmissibility, contact rates and infectious duration. The effective reproduction number, often written with a time subscript, is the quantity surveillance actually estimates, reflecting accumulated immunity, behaviour and interventions. Estimation methods include fitting compartmental models, renewal equation approaches that combine the time series of cases with an assumed generation interval distribution, and phylodynamic birth-death models that infer the ratio of transmission to removal from sequence data and sampling times. Each approach is sensitive to its inputs: case-based estimates depend on testing rates and reporting delays, while sequence-based estimates depend on sampling intensity and on the molecular clock. Averages also conceal heterogeneity, since many infections produce no onward transmission while a minority produce many, so the same mean is compatible with very different epidemic behaviour. Estimates are population-specific and time-specific; quoting a single value for a pathogen without stating the setting, period and method is not meaningful.
practical_example: An analyst preparing a weekly situation report estimates the effective reproduction number from reported cases using a renewal method, and separately from genomic data using a birth-death model. The two estimates overlap in their credible intervals but the genomic estimate is less affected by a change in testing policy that week. Both are reported, with their assumptions stated.
common_misunderstanding: R0 is often quoted as a fixed property of a pathogen, as though it were a constant like a melting point. It depends on contact patterns, population structure and immunity, so it differs between settings and over time. The abbreviation is also used loosely for the effective reproduction number, which is a different quantity and should be labelled separately.

plain_definition: Sanger sequencing is a laboratory method for reading the order of bases along one short stretch of DNA, typically a few hundred letters at a time. Copying of the stretch is deliberately stopped at random positions by special building blocks, and the resulting fragments are sorted by length so that the base at each position can be read off in turn.
technical_explanation: Sanger sequencing uses a DNA polymerase to copy a template from a defined primer in the presence of ordinary deoxynucleotides plus a small proportion of fluorescently labelled dideoxynucleotides, which lack the chemical group needed to extend the chain. Each incorporation of a dideoxynucleotide terminates that molecule, so the reaction generates a nested set of fragments differing by one base. Capillary electrophoresis separates the fragments by size and a detector records the colour of the terminating base, producing a chromatogram whose peaks are translated into a base sequence with an associated quality value. Usable read lengths of several hundred bases per reaction are routine. The method remains the reference standard for interrogating a single locus because its per-base accuracy is high and the trace can be inspected by eye. Its limitations are equally important: it reads one amplicon per reaction, so it scales poorly; it reports the mixture of molecules in the reaction, so a low-fraction somatic variant can be hidden in the background of the trace; and it cannot resolve which of two heterozygous positions lie on the same chromosome without further work.
practical_example: A diagnostic laboratory finds a candidate single-nucleotide variant in a gene panel run on a patient sample. Before the result is reported, staff design primers around the position, amplify that fragment from the stored DNA extract and read it by Sanger sequencing. Seeing the same base change in the chromatogram, from an independent amplification, confirms the finding is not an artefact of the panel chemistry.
common_misunderstanding: Many readers assume Sanger sequencing has been retired by newer platforms. It has not. It is still the practical choice for confirming a single position, checking a cloned insert or typing one short region, and many laboratories use it daily. What it cannot do is survey a whole genome affordably or reliably detect variants present in only a small fraction of the molecules sequenced.

plain_definition: Next-generation sequencing, abbreviated NGS, is a family of methods that read millions of DNA fragments at the same time instead of one at a time. The sample is broken into pieces, prepared into a sequencing library and loaded onto an instrument that reads every fragment in parallel. Computers then assemble or map those reads to work out the original sequence.
technical_explanation: Next-generation sequencing covers the massively parallel platforms that displaced single-amplicon chemistry for most genome-scale work. The common pattern is the same across chemistries: nucleic acid is fragmented or amplified into defined pieces, adapters are ligated or added by tagmentation, the resulting library is immobilised or loaded, and many millions of templates are read simultaneously. Output is a set of reads with per-base quality scores, usually in FASTQ format, which are mapped to a reference or assembled de novo. The term is deliberately broad and now covers both short-read and long-read instruments, so stating the platform and chemistry is more informative than the label itself. The practical consequence of parallelism is that depth and breadth become design choices rather than fixed properties: the same instrument can read one genome deeply or hundreds of amplicons shallowly. Limitations follow from the workflow rather than the detector. Amplification introduces duplicate and composition biases, short fragments cannot span long repeats, index misassignment can move reads between multiplexed samples, and every step from extraction onwards contributes error that the quality score alone does not capture.
practical_example: A public health laboratory sequences several hundred bacterial isolates collected during a hospital outbreak investigation. Each isolate is extracted, prepared as a barcoded library, and the libraries are pooled onto a single run. One instrument run yields enough data for every isolate to be assembled and compared, which would have been impossible one fragment at a time.
common_misunderstanding: A frequent error is to treat next-generation sequencing as a single technology with one accuracy figure. It is a category covering several chemistries with different read lengths, error profiles and costs. Accuracy also depends on the library, the depth and the region being read, so a claim about sequencing performance means little until the platform, the workflow and the target are specified.

plain_definition: Short-read sequencing reads DNA in small pieces, usually between about fifty and three hundred bases each, but reads enormous numbers of those pieces at once. Because each piece is short, software must work out where it came from by matching it against a reference sequence. The approach is accurate per base and inexpensive per sample.
technical_explanation: Short-read platforms fragment nucleic acid, attach adapters, and read each fragment from one or both ends to a fixed length set by the chemistry. Per-base accuracy is high and the cost per gigabase is low, which is why short reads underpin most population sequencing, exome and panel testing, RNA quantification and bacterial genomics. The analytical price is ambiguity of placement. A read shorter than a repeat unit cannot be assigned uniquely within that repeat, so mapping quality collapses in segmental duplications, long tandem arrays and paralogous gene families, and structural rearrangements are inferred indirectly from coverage changes and discordant read pairs rather than observed directly. Amplification during library preparation and cluster generation introduces duplicates and under-represents regions of extreme base composition, particularly those that are very GC-rich or GC-poor. Paired-end reads, longer inserts and linked-read or long-read supplementation each mitigate part of this, but none removes it. Reporting should therefore state read length, insert size and depth, since those parameters, not the platform name, determine which variant classes the experiment could have detected.
practical_example: A research group sequences tumour and matched blood samples to a high depth using short reads to call somatic single-nucleotide variants and small insertions and deletions. When the same data are used to look for a suspected large rearrangement, the evidence is indirect, and the group adds a long-read run on the remaining material to resolve the breakpoints.
common_misunderstanding: It is tempting to read high per-base accuracy as whole-genome completeness. The two are different. Short reads are individually accurate yet systematically blind to parts of the genome where they cannot be placed unambiguously, so a region can be absent from the results not because it is unchanged but because no read could be confidently mapped there.

plain_definition: Long-read sequencing reads very long stretches of DNA in one piece, often tens of thousands of bases, rather than many short fragments. Long reads can span repeated regions and large rearrangements that short reads cannot cross, so they make assembly and structural analysis easier. Historically they made more errors per base, although the chemistries have improved substantially.
technical_explanation: Long-read platforms read single molecules without the short fixed read length imposed by cyclic short-read chemistry. Two approaches dominate in practice: single-molecule real-time sequencing, which observes a polymerase incorporating labelled nucleotides and can read the same circular template repeatedly to build a highly accurate consensus, and nanopore sequencing, which reads an intact strand as it passes through a pore. Read lengths are limited mainly by the length of the input molecules, so high-molecular-weight extraction becomes the critical laboratory step. Long reads resolve repeats, segmental duplications and structural variants directly, enable phasing of variants across long haplotype blocks, support contiguous de novo assembly, and in some chemistries detect base modifications such as methylation without a separate bisulfite step. Limitations remain: raw per-read error is higher than for short reads unless consensus or repeat-pass strategies are applied, homopolymer runs are a recurring difficulty, cost per base is higher, and the requirement for intact long molecules makes degraded or formalin-fixed material a poor substrate.
practical_example: A laboratory investigating a suspected large duplication in a family cannot determine its orientation or breakpoints from short-read coverage alone. Using carefully extracted high-molecular-weight DNA, long reads spanning the whole rearrangement are generated, and single reads crossing both junctions show the orientation directly rather than by inference.
common_misunderstanding: Long reads are often described as simply better than short reads. The trade is one of properties, not quality. Long reads provide contiguity and direct observation of structure; short reads provide low cost and high per-base accuracy at depth. The right choice depends on whether the question concerns single bases or the arrangement of large segments.

plain_definition: Nanopore sequencing reads DNA or RNA by pulling a single strand through a tiny protein pore in a membrane. As each part of the strand passes through, it changes an electrical current in a characteristic way, and software converts that changing signal into a sequence of bases. The devices are small and produce data as the run proceeds.
technical_explanation: Nanopore sequencing measures the ionic current through a biological pore held in an electrically resistant membrane as a nucleic acid strand is ratcheted through by a motor protein. The current is modulated by the stretch of bases occupying the pore, and a neural network model converts the raw signal trace into base calls. Because the strand is read intact, read length is set by the input molecule rather than the chemistry, and reads of tens to hundreds of kilobases are achievable with careful extraction. Data stream in real time, which allows a run to be stopped once sufficient coverage is reached and supports adaptive sampling, where a target region is enriched by rejecting unwanted molecules at the pore. Native strands are read directly, so base modifications can be inferred from the signal. The instruments are portable and have been used for field pathogen surveillance. Limitations include higher raw per-read error than short-read platforms, systematic difficulty with homopolymer runs, dependence of accuracy on the basecalling model version, and sensitivity of yield to DNA purity and pore occupancy.
practical_example: During an outbreak response in a district laboratory with limited infrastructure, amplicons from patient samples are barcoded, loaded onto a portable nanopore device and sequenced on site. Consensus genomes are generated within the same working day and shared with the national reference laboratory, informing the investigation while transport of samples to a central facility would still have been in progress.
common_misunderstanding: Because nanopore devices are small and inexpensive, they are sometimes assumed to be lower-grade instruments. Portability is a design choice, not a measure of data quality. What genuinely differs is the error profile: errors are distributed differently from short-read platforms and depend on the basecalling model, so the analysis chosen must suit that profile rather than being transferred unchanged.

plain_definition: Sequencing by synthesis works out a DNA sequence by watching a new strand being built against it. The instrument adds labelled building blocks one cycle at a time, records which base was added at each position by its colour or by another signal, and repeats. Doing this for millions of fragments at once is what makes modern sequencing fast.
technical_explanation: Sequencing by synthesis is the family of chemistries in which base identity is read out as a polymerase extends a primer along a template. In the cyclic reversible-termination form used by most short-read instruments, each fragment is amplified into a local cluster of identical copies, and each cycle adds one labelled, reversibly blocked nucleotide per template. The instrument images the flow cell, then cleaves the label and the blocking group so the next cycle can proceed. Base calls accumulate cycle by cycle, with a quality score reflecting the confidence of each call. Single-molecule real-time sequencing is also synthesis-based but observes incorporation continuously in a single immobilised polymerase rather than in cycles. Characteristic limitations follow from the cycling itself: phasing errors, where molecules within a cluster fall out of step, accumulate with cycle number and cause quality to decline towards the end of a read; signal from neighbouring clusters can bleed across; and because clusters originate from amplification, duplicate fragments and composition bias enter before any base is read.
practical_example: A core facility reviews the quality report from a completed run and sees per-base quality falling steadily across the final cycles of each read, in every sample on the flow cell. Recognising this as the expected behaviour of cycle-by-cycle chemistry rather than a fault with any one library, the team trims the low-quality read ends before mapping.
common_misunderstanding: The term is often used as though it meant one manufacturer's instrument. It describes a principle, shared by several chemistries that differ in how the incorporation signal is detected and whether reading proceeds in discrete cycles. Equating sequencing by synthesis with a single platform obscures those differences, which determine read length and error behaviour.

plain_definition: Library preparation is the set of laboratory steps that turns extracted DNA or RNA into a form a sequencing instrument can read. The material is cut or copied into fragments of suitable length, short known sequences called adapters are attached to the ends, and sample-specific barcodes are added. The quality of this step largely determines the quality of the data.
technical_explanation: Library preparation converts purified nucleic acid into adapter-flanked fragments of a defined size distribution with the sequences required for binding, priming and indexing. Typical steps are fragmentation by sonication, enzymatic digestion or tagmentation; end repair and adenylation where ligation chemistry demands it; adapter ligation or addition during a tagmentation reaction; optional amplification; and size selection by beads or gel. RNA workflows add reverse transcription and some form of selection, commonly polyadenylated transcript capture or ribosomal RNA depletion, each of which changes which transcripts are represented. Target enrichment by hybridisation capture or multiplex amplification is inserted here when only part of the genome is wanted. The protocol determines what the data can show: insert size sets the span of paired reads, amplification cycles set the duplicate rate and composition bias, and fragmentation chemistry introduces its own position preferences. Low-input and degraded samples amplify these effects, since fewer starting molecules mean that stochastic loss of templates, rather than sequencing error, limits what can be detected.
practical_example: A laboratory processing degraded archival tissue finds that libraries from those samples carry far more duplicate reads than libraries from fresh blood on the same run. The cause is the small number of intact starting molecules, which are then amplified heavily. The team reduces amplification cycles and raises the input amount where material allows, instead of simply sequencing deeper.
common_misunderstanding: Library preparation is often seen as routine sample handling with the real measurement happening on the instrument. In reality most of the bias in a sequencing dataset is introduced before loading: fragment size, amplification, enrichment chemistry and the RNA selection method all decide which molecules are present to be read at all.

plain_definition: Multiplexing means sequencing many samples together in one run. Each sample is given its own short identifying sequence, called a barcode or index, during library preparation. After the run, software sorts the reads back to the sample they came from by reading those barcodes, a step called demultiplexing. This shares the cost of a run across many samples.
technical_explanation: Multiplexing adds a sample-specific index sequence to every fragment of a library so that pooled libraries can be separated computationally after sequencing. Indices sit within or adjacent to the adapters, and modern designs place a distinct index at each end, the dual-index arrangement, because a single index is vulnerable to misassignment. Index hopping, in which free adapters or index primers transfer between libraries on a patterned flow cell, moves a small fraction of reads into the wrong sample; unique dual indices allow such reads to be identified and discarded rather than silently counted. Index sets are also chosen for sequence diversity and for an edit distance that permits error correction. Practical design involves balancing the number of samples against the depth each requires, since the run yield is divided among the pool, and ensuring the pool is quantified accurately so that libraries are represented evenly. The consequences of failure are specific: uneven pooling produces samples with insufficient depth, while misassignment can introduce low-level contaminating reads that mimic genuine low-fraction variants.
practical_example: A surveillance laboratory pools ninety-six barcoded pathogen libraries onto one flow cell. After demultiplexing, three samples have far fewer reads than the rest. Reviewing the pooling records shows those three libraries were quantified before a repeat amplification step, so they entered the pool at a lower concentration and are repeated on the next run.
common_misunderstanding: A natural assumption is that demultiplexing returns every read to its true sample. A small proportion is misassigned, through index hopping or sequencing error in the index itself. This matters most when looking for rare variants or for pathogen reads at low abundance, where a handful of misassigned reads can be mistaken for a genuine finding.

plain_definition: A sequencing adapter is a short, known piece of DNA attached to each end of a fragment during library preparation. It is not part of the sample. Adapters give the instrument somewhere to bind the fragment and start reading, and they usually carry the barcode that identifies the sample. Adapter sequence is removed before analysis.
technical_explanation: Adapters are synthetic oligonucleotide constructs ligated or transposed onto library fragments to supply every function the instrument requires outside the insert itself: a sequence complementary to the flow cell or bead, a priming site for the sequencing reaction, and one or two index sequences for demultiplexing. Designs vary, with Y-shaped and hairpin forms used to control which strand is read and to keep the two ends distinguishable. Because adapters are a fixed, known sequence, their presence in the data is diagnostic. When the insert is shorter than the read length, the polymerase reads through the insert into the opposite adapter, and that adapter sequence appears at the end of the read; left in place it will fail to map or, worse, map spuriously. Trimming tools detect and remove these sequences before alignment. Adapters also create artefacts when they self-ligate, producing adapter dimers that consume capacity on the instrument without yielding useful data, which is why size selection and library quality checks look for them specifically.
practical_example: A technologist reviewing a quality report for an RNA library sees adapter sequence detected in a large proportion of reads. The insert size distribution confirms the fragments were shorter than the configured read length, so reads ran off the end of the insert. Trimming the adapters restores normal mapping rates without repeating the run.
common_misunderstanding: Adapters are sometimes mistaken for part of the sequenced organism, especially by newcomers who blast an untrimmed read and find no match. Adapter sequence is added in the laboratory and carries no biological information from the sample. Equally, removing adapters is not optional tidying: untrimmed adapter sequence distorts mapping and downstream quantification.

plain_definition: A read is one stretch of sequence produced by a sequencing instrument from a single fragment of DNA or RNA. Each read is a string of bases together with a quality value for every base, indicating how confident the instrument is in that call. A sequencing run produces millions of reads, which analysis software then maps or assembles.
technical_explanation: A read is the atomic unit of sequencing output: the base calls derived from one template molecule or one cluster of identical copies, with per-base quality scores, conventionally stored in FASTQ format. Read length is set by the chemistry, from tens of bases on some short-read configurations to hundreds of kilobases on single-molecule platforms. Reads are not observations of the genome directly; they are observations of library molecules, so they inherit every bias introduced during extraction, fragmentation, enrichment and amplification. Several reads can also derive from the same original molecule after amplification, and these duplicates must be marked so that they are not counted as independent evidence for a variant. Downstream, a read acquires a mapping position and a mapping quality describing the confidence that it came from that locus, which is a separate quantity from the base quality. Reads that fail to map, map to many places, or map with low confidence are not necessarily errors; they frequently indicate repetitive sequence, contamination, or genuine divergence from the reference used.
practical_example: A bioinformatician inspects a surveillance dataset and finds that a quarter of reads in one sample fail to map to the expected pathogen reference. Classifying the unmapped reads shows them to be host sequence carried through extraction. The run itself was sound; the sample simply contained a mixture, and the effective depth on the target was lower than the raw read count implied.
common_misunderstanding: The raw number of reads is often treated as the measure of how much data a sample yielded. It is not, on its own. Reads can be duplicates of one another, can come from contaminating material, or can be unmappable. What matters is how many independent, correctly placed reads cover the region being studied.

plain_definition: Paired-end sequencing reads each DNA fragment from both of its ends rather than from one end only. The two reads come from the same molecule and are a roughly known distance apart, which helps software place them correctly and reveals when that distance is unexpected. Reading from one end only is called single-end sequencing.
technical_explanation: In paired-end sequencing the instrument reads the first strand of a library fragment, regenerates the template, and reads the opposite end, producing two reads of known orientation separated by the unsequenced middle of the insert. The pair provides two kinds of extra information. First, placement: a read that is individually ambiguous can often be anchored by its mate, improving effective mapping in repetitive regions. Second, structural evidence: because the library has a characteristic insert size distribution, pairs that map too far apart, too close together, in the wrong orientation, or to different chromosomes are candidate signatures of deletions, insertions, inversions and translocations. Paired reads also allow overlapping mates from short inserts to be merged into a single more accurate consensus read, which is useful in amplicon work. The advantages depend entirely on the insert size being appropriate and well controlled, so poor size selection removes most of the benefit. Discordant pairs are evidence, not proof, since mismapping and reference assembly errors generate the same patterns.
practical_example: A laboratory analysing a tumour sample observes a cluster of read pairs whose two ends map to different chromosomes, all pointing to the same two positions. Taken together these discordant pairs suggest a translocation, which is then confirmed by an orthogonal assay before the finding is included in any report.
common_misunderstanding: Paired-end data are sometimes described as doubling the read length. They do not: the middle of the fragment is never read. What a pair provides is two separated observations from one molecule with a known expected distance between them, which aids placement and reveals structural changes, not a single continuous longer sequence.

synonyms: depth of coverage; sequencing depth; coverage depth
plain_definition: Read depth is the number of sequencing reads that cover a particular position in the genome. A position covered by thirty reads is said to have thirty-fold depth. Greater depth gives more confidence that a difference seen at that position is real rather than an error, and it is usually reported as an average across the target region.
technical_explanation: Read depth at a position is the count of reads overlapping it after mapping and, conventionally, after duplicate marking and quality filtering, so raw and filtered depth can differ substantially. Depth determines the statistical power to detect a variant and the confidence with which a genotype is assigned: detecting a heterozygous germline variant reliably requires far less depth than detecting a somatic variant present in a small fraction of molecules, which is why tumour and cell-free DNA assays are run at much higher depth than germline genome sequencing. Depth is never uniform. Composition bias, capture efficiency, mappability and amplification all create regions that are systematically shallow, so a mean depth across a target conceals the distribution that actually matters. Laboratories therefore specify minimum depth per base and the proportion of target bases meeting it, rather than an average alone. Increasing depth has limits: it reduces sampling error but cannot overcome systematic artefacts, and beyond the point where errors are correlated rather than independent, additional reads add little information.
practical_example: A diagnostic panel specifies that every reported base must be covered by at least a stated minimum number of reads. In one sample the mean depth across the panel is comfortably high, yet two exons fall below the threshold because of a difficult base composition. Those exons are filled in by a separate amplicon assay rather than reported as uninformative.
common_misunderstanding: Mean depth is often taken as a guarantee that every target base was adequately read. Coverage is uneven, so a high average can coexist with regions that have almost no reads. A region with insufficient depth has not been shown to be free of variants; it has simply not been examined properly, and the two should never be reported as equivalent.

synonyms: breadth of coverage; percentage coverage; genome coverage
plain_definition: Breadth of coverage is the proportion of the target region that was read at all, or that reached a stated minimum depth. It answers a different question from read depth: not how many times a position was read, but how much of the intended region was covered. It is usually reported as a percentage of target bases.
technical_explanation: Breadth of coverage quantifies completeness of a sequencing experiment against a defined target, whether that target is a whole genome, an exome, a panel or a pathogen reference. It is normally expressed as the fraction of target bases reaching a threshold depth, for instance the proportion of panel bases covered at least twenty-fold, since breadth without a depth qualifier is ambiguous. Breadth and depth are independent axes: a shallow whole-genome run can have excellent breadth and poor depth, while a deep amplicon panel has the reverse. In pathogen genomics breadth drives whether a consensus genome can be called at all, and incomplete breadth produces stretches of ambiguous bases that affect lineage assignment and phylogenetic placement. Breadth is limited by capture or amplicon design, by sample quality and input quantity, and by mappability, because reads from repetitive or paralogous sequence cannot be placed uniquely. Reporting breadth honestly means stating the target definition used, since the same data give different percentages against a coding region, a padded panel or a whole genome.
practical_example: A sequencing facility processing viral samples with varying amounts of material reports, for each sample, the percentage of the reference genome covered at the laboratory's minimum depth. Samples falling below the stated threshold are flagged as partial genomes and excluded from lineage assignment, rather than being reported with long runs of ambiguous bases.
common_misunderstanding: Coverage is frequently quoted as a single number without saying whether depth or breadth is meant, and the two are sometimes used interchangeably. They are not the same. Thirty-fold depth says how intensively covered bases were read; ninety-five per cent breadth says how much of the target was reached. A result needs both figures to be interpretable.

synonyms: Phred score; base quality score; Q score
plain_definition: A Phred quality score tells you how confident a sequencing instrument is about a single base it has called. The scale is logarithmic: a score of twenty means roughly a one in a hundred chance the base is wrong, thirty means one in a thousand, and forty one in ten thousand. Every base in a read carries one.
technical_explanation: The Phred score Q is defined as minus ten times the base-ten logarithm of the estimated probability that the base call is incorrect, so each increase of ten corresponds to a tenfold reduction in that estimated error probability. Scores are encoded as single ASCII characters on the quality line of a FASTQ record. They are estimates produced by the instrument's calling model, calibrated against training data, and they can be miscalibrated for an unusual sample, chemistry or basecaller version; recalibration steps in variant-calling pipelines exist precisely because the raw values drift from observed error rates. Quality typically declines along a read in cycle-based chemistries, and quality-based trimming or filtering is standard before mapping. Two cautions matter in interpretation. The score describes the instrument's confidence in reading that molecule; it says nothing about whether the molecule faithfully represents the sample, so a polymerase error during library amplification can be read with high confidence. It is also distinct from mapping quality, which uses the same scale but describes confidence in a read's genomic position.
practical_example: A bioinformatician comparing two runs sees average base quality dropping sharply after a certain cycle in one of them. Rather than discarding the run, the affected read ends are trimmed and the data are mapped and compared with the other run, which confirms that the usable portion of the reads supports the same genotypes.
common_misunderstanding: A high quality score is often read as proof that a variant is real. It is not. The score describes confidence in reading one base from one molecule, so an error introduced earlier, during amplification or by a chimeric library fragment, will carry a high score. Variant confidence comes from independent supporting reads and the calling model, not from base quality alone.

plain_definition: The polymerase chain reaction, abbreviated PCR, is a laboratory method that makes many copies of a chosen piece of DNA. Short synthetic primers mark the start and end of the region, and repeated cycles of heating and cooling let an enzyme copy it again and again. A small amount of starting material can become enough to detect or sequence.
technical_explanation: PCR amplifies a defined region exponentially through repeated thermal cycles of denaturation, primer annealing and extension by a thermostable DNA polymerase. Specificity comes from the primer pair, which must bind the intended flanking sequences and not elsewhere; sensitivity comes from the exponential increase, which in principle allows a single template molecule to be detected. Variants of the method extend its reach: reverse transcription PCR converts RNA to complementary DNA first, multiplex PCR amplifies many targets in one reaction, and digital PCR partitions the reaction to count molecules absolutely. PCR underpins much of modern genomics, from amplicon sequencing and library amplification to diagnostic detection of pathogens. Its limitations are well characterised. Primer binding sites can carry variants that reduce or abolish amplification, producing a false negative in a diagnostic assay or a dropout in an amplicon panel. The polymerase introduces errors that are then amplified, and amplification is not perfectly even across templates, so the proportions of products do not reliably reflect the proportions of input molecules. The extreme sensitivity also makes carry-over contamination a constant risk.
practical_example: A surveillance laboratory using a tiled amplicon scheme to sequence a virus notices one amplicon failing repeatedly in recently collected samples. Inspection shows a variant beneath a primer binding site in the circulating lineage. The primer scheme is updated, and in the interim the affected region is reported as ambiguous rather than as reference sequence.
common_misunderstanding: PCR is widely assumed to be an all-or-nothing test of whether a sequence is present. Failure to amplify has several explanations besides absence of the target: a variant under a primer site, inhibitors carried through extraction, degraded material or too little input. Equally, a product does not prove viable organism, only that the target sequence was present.

plain_definition: Quantitative PCR, abbreviated qPCR, measures how much of a target sequence is present while the copying reaction is running, rather than only looking at the end product. A fluorescent signal rises as copies accumulate, and the cycle at which it becomes detectable indicates how much target was there at the start. More starting material gives an earlier signal.
technical_explanation: Quantitative PCR monitors amplification in real time using either an intercalating dye that binds double-stranded product or a sequence-specific hydrolysis probe that releases fluorescence when cleaved during extension. The cycle at which fluorescence crosses a defined threshold is inversely related to the logarithm of the starting template quantity. Absolute quantification uses a standard curve of known concentrations; relative quantification compares a target to a reference gene between conditions. When the target is RNA, reverse transcription precedes amplification, and the efficiency of that step becomes part of the measurement. Assay performance is characterised by amplification efficiency, linear dynamic range and limit of detection, and controls for extraction, inhibition and contamination are integral rather than optional. Important limitations: results are comparative within an assay and platform, so values are not transferable between laboratories without calibration against a common standard; probe or primer mismatches caused by variants reduce apparent quantity; and inhibitors carried through extraction shift results in ways that an internal control is designed to expose. Note that the abbreviation RT can mean either reverse transcription or real time, and usage should be stated explicitly.
practical_example: A laboratory measuring expression of a gene across treated and untreated cell cultures runs qPCR with two stably expressed reference genes alongside the target. Reporting the difference between conditions relative to those references, rather than raw cycle values, allows the comparison to survive differences in extraction yield between the cultures.
common_misunderstanding: Because qPCR produces a number, that number is often treated as an absolute measurement of how much material was present. Without a standard curve it is a relative quantity, specific to the assay, the extraction and the instrument. Comparing raw cycle values between laboratories, or between assays targeting different regions, is not meaningful.

synonyms: DNA extraction; RNA extraction; nucleic acid purification
plain_definition: Nucleic acid extraction is the process of getting DNA or RNA out of a sample and into a clean solution that later methods can use. Cells are broken open, proteins and other material are removed, and the nucleic acid is captured, washed and released. How well this is done sets a ceiling on everything that follows.
technical_explanation: Extraction releases nucleic acid from cells or virions and separates it from proteins, lipids, polysaccharides and inhibitory compounds. Common formats include silica membrane columns, magnetic beads suited to automation, and organic separation methods. The chemistry chosen determines what is recovered: methods optimised for total nucleic acid recover both DNA and RNA, column methods can deplete very short fragments such as cell-free DNA, and vigorous bead beating needed for tough-walled organisms shears high-molecular-weight DNA that long-read sequencing requires. RNA work adds the constraint that ribonucleases are ubiquitous and active, so cold chain, stabilising reagents and clean technique matter from the moment of collection. Outputs are assessed for yield, purity by absorbance ratios, and integrity by electrophoretic or microfluidic sizing. Known limitations include differential lysis, which skews microbial community composition in metagenomic studies; carry-over of inhibitors such as haem or humic substances that suppress amplification; and loss of material at low input, where the physical adsorption of molecules to plastic becomes significant.
practical_example: A laboratory preparing samples for long-read sequencing finds read lengths much shorter than expected. The extraction protocol in use involved vigorous vortexing and narrow pipette tips, both of which shear long molecules. Switching to a gentle, wide-bore protocol designed for high-molecular-weight DNA increases read length without changing the sequencing chemistry.
common_misunderstanding: Extraction is often treated as a neutral preparatory step that simply makes the sample usable. The method actively shapes the result: it decides which fragment sizes survive, which organisms in a mixture are lysed efficiently, and whether inhibitors remain. A difference between two datasets can originate entirely in the extraction protocol rather than in the biology.

plain_definition: Sample quality control is the set of checks that confirm material is good enough to proceed at each stage of a laboratory workflow. Typical checks measure how much nucleic acid is present, how pure it is, how intact it is, and whether the library has the expected fragment sizes. Failing samples are repeated or reported as uninformative.
technical_explanation: Quality control in a sequencing workflow is layered. At the sample stage, fluorometric quantification measures nucleic acid specifically, whereas absorbance measures anything that absorbs at the same wavelength and is therefore a purity indicator rather than a reliable quantity; integrity is assessed by automated electrophoresis, giving metrics such as an RNA integrity number or a DNA integrity score. At the library stage, fragment size distribution and molar concentration determine loading and reveal adapter dimers or over-amplification. After sequencing, read-level metrics cover base quality by cycle, adapter content, duplicate rate, base composition, mapping rate, depth and breadth against the target, and for human samples, checks of sex concordance and of identity against an independent genotype. Thresholds must be set for the assay rather than copied between assays, since acceptable input for a high-depth panel differs from that for shallow whole-genome sequencing. The essential discipline is that failing checks lead to repetition or to an explicit uninformative result; silently reporting a sample that fell below threshold converts a known limitation into an unrecognised error.
practical_example: A laboratory establishing an RNA sequencing service sets a minimum integrity score for accepted samples. Early batches from a collaborating clinic fail consistently, and reviewing collection practice shows a delay before stabilisation of the specimens. Changing the collection protocol, rather than lowering the threshold, resolves the problem for subsequent batches.
common_misunderstanding: Quality control is sometimes seen as a hurdle to be cleared so that analysis can start. Its purpose is to decide which results can be trusted and which cannot. A sample that passes every check can still produce poor data in a difficult region, and a sample that fails one metric may still be informative for a narrower question, provided the limitation is stated.

plain_definition: Whole-genome sequencing, abbreviated WGS, reads essentially the entire genome of an organism rather than selected parts of it. For a human sample that means both the coding regions and the much larger non-coding fraction; for a bacterium or virus it usually means the complete genome. It provides the broadest view a sequencing experiment can give.
technical_explanation: Whole-genome sequencing generates reads across the genome without target selection, so coverage depends on library chemistry and mappability rather than on a capture design. Human applications are typically run at a modest uniform depth sufficient to genotype germline variants, while microbial genomes are sequenced to much higher relative depth because the genomes are small. Compared with exome or panel approaches, whole-genome data cover regulatory and intronic sequence, give more even coverage because no hybridisation step is involved, and support detection of structural and copy-number variation as well as mitochondrial and, in pathogens, plasmid content. The constraints are analytical and interpretive rather than technical. Most variants found lie outside coding sequence, where evidence for functional consequence is sparse, so the yield of interpretable findings does not rise in proportion to the number of variants detected. Short-read whole-genome data still miss repetitive and segmentally duplicated regions, and comparison depends on a reference whose composition shapes which variants are even representable, a limitation that pangenome references are intended to reduce.
practical_example: A national public health laboratory sequences complete genomes of bacterial isolates from several hospitals. Because the whole genome is available, investigators can compare isolates at single-base resolution, type them by their core genes, and screen the same data for resistance determinants and plasmid sequences, without running a separate assay for each question.
common_misunderstanding: Whole-genome sequencing is often assumed to detect every variant in a sample. It does not. Coverage is incomplete in repetitive and difficult regions, short reads resolve some structural changes poorly, and variants absent from the reference framework may not be represented at all. Breadth of sequencing should not be confused with completeness of detection or of interpretation.

synonyms: gene panel; targeted sequencing; panel testing
plain_definition: Targeted panel sequencing reads only a chosen set of genes or regions instead of the whole genome. The regions are captured or amplified before sequencing, so most of the data come from the targets. Concentrating the reading effort on a small target allows much greater depth for the same cost, which matters when looking for rare or low-level variants.
technical_explanation: Panels enrich a defined target before or during library preparation, either by hybridisation capture with biotinylated probes or by multiplex amplification of the target regions. Enrichment allows depth that would be unaffordable genome-wide, which is why panels dominate somatic tumour testing, cell-free DNA assays and pathogen resistance typing, where detecting variants at low allele fraction is the point. A panel is a deliberate restriction: it can only report on content within its design, so its gene list, exon boundaries and padding define its clinical scope, and a negative result means no reportable variant was found in those regions. Enrichment also introduces its own behaviour. Capture efficiency varies by probe, leaving some exons reliably shallow; amplicon designs are vulnerable to variants under primer sites and generally detect copy-number and structural changes poorly; and both approaches require validation of each region against a reference material. Panels age as knowledge changes, so the design, its version and its measured per-base coverage should accompany any result.

A clinician asks whether a gene outside the panel was altered. The laboratory explains that this gene was never interrogated, so the result is silent about it rather than negative for it.
common_misunderstanding: A negative panel result is frequently read as the absence of any relevant variant. It means only that no reportable variant was detected within the regions the panel covers, at the depth achieved. Genes outside the design, intronic and regulatory sequence, and variant types the chemistry detects poorly, such as large rearrangements, are simply not examined.

plain_definition: RNA sequencing, abbreviated RNA-Seq, reads the RNA molecules present in a sample to show which genes are being expressed and at what relative level. The RNA is converted to DNA, prepared as a sequencing library and read, and the resulting reads are counted against genes or transcripts. It captures a snapshot of activity at the moment of collection.
technical_explanation: RNA sequencing quantifies the transcriptome by converting RNA to complementary DNA, preparing a library and counting reads assigned to genes or transcripts. Library choice determines what is observed: selection of polyadenylated transcripts captures most messenger RNA but excludes many non-polyadenylated species, while ribosomal depletion retains a broader population, including unprocessed and non-coding transcripts, at the cost of more complex data. Reads are either aligned to a genome with a splice-aware aligner or assigned to transcripts by selective alignment, and counts are normalised for library size and composition before comparison. Differential expression is assessed with count-based models that account for the mean-variance relationship of such data. Beyond expression, the data support detection of splicing changes, fusion transcripts and expressed variants. Limitations are substantial and routinely understated. Counts are relative within a library, so a global shift in transcription is invisible without external spike-in controls; reverse transcription, amplification and fragment-length effects introduce bias; the reference annotation constrains what can be quantified; and expression differences describe association with condition, not a causal mechanism.
practical_example: A research group compares bladder tumour tissue with adjacent non-tumour tissue from the same resections, sequencing RNA from both. Genes showing consistent differences between the two tissue types across several pairs become candidates for follow-up, and the group confirms a subset by an independent assay before drawing conclusions about the pathway involved.
common_misunderstanding: Differences in RNA levels are often reported as if they explained a phenotype. An expression difference is an association measured at one moment in a particular tissue. It may be a cause, a consequence, or a correlate of something else entirely, and transcript level does not reliably predict protein level, so further evidence is required before any mechanistic claim.

plain_definition: Single-cell RNA sequencing, abbreviated scRNA-Seq, measures gene activity in individual cells rather than averaging across a whole tissue. Cells are separated, each one's RNA is tagged with a unique label, and everything is sequenced together. The labels let software reconstruct which reads came from which cell, revealing the different cell types present in a sample.
technical_explanation: Single-cell RNA sequencing resolves transcription at the level of individual cells by isolating them, most commonly in droplets, and attaching a cell barcode and a unique molecular identifier to each captured transcript before amplification. Unique molecular identifiers allow duplicate reads from amplification to be collapsed into molecule counts. The resulting matrix of cells by genes is sparse, because only a fraction of transcripts in each cell is captured, and analysis proceeds through quality filtering, normalisation, dimensionality reduction, clustering and annotation of clusters against marker genes. Applications include defining cell-type composition, identifying rare populations, and studying heterogeneity within a tumour. Several limitations shape interpretation. Tissue dissociation stresses cells and destroys fragile types selectively, so the recovered composition is not necessarily the composition in the tissue. Droplets containing two cells produce artefactual mixed profiles, ambient RNA contaminates all barcodes, and cluster boundaries depend on analytical parameters rather than on a natural discreteness of cell states. Single-nucleus protocols address some dissociation problems, at the cost of losing cytoplasmic transcripts.
practical_example: A group studying a tumour biopsy dissociates the tissue and profiles thousands of individual cells, finding clusters corresponding to malignant cells, fibroblasts and several immune populations. The proportion of each type is interpreted cautiously, because cells differ in how well they survive dissociation, and the group checks key populations against stained tissue sections.
common_misunderstanding: Clusters produced by single-cell analysis are easily mistaken for discrete, naturally defined cell types. They are groupings produced by a chosen set of analytical parameters, applied to cells that survived dissociation. Changing resolution settings changes the number of clusters, and the cells present in the data are not necessarily a faithful sample of those in the tissue.

synonyms: DNA microarray; SNP array; expression array; chip
plain_definition: A microarray is a slide or chip carrying many thousands of short known DNA sequences arranged in fixed positions. Labelled material from a sample sticks to the spots that match it, and the pattern of signal shows which sequences were present and in what quantity. Arrays measure predetermined targets rather than reading sequence directly.
technical_explanation: A microarray measures hybridisation of labelled sample nucleic acid to immobilised probes of known sequence. Genotyping arrays interrogate a fixed set of chosen positions, usually common single-nucleotide polymorphisms, and remain the standard tool for genome-wide association studies and for the genotype data behind polygenic scores, largely because the cost per sample is low and the output is highly standardised. Expression arrays measure transcript abundance from probe intensity, and array comparative genomic hybridisation detects copy-number change across the genome. Signal is continuous and relative, so processing involves background correction, normalisation across arrays and summarisation of multiple probes per feature before statistical analysis. The defining limitation is that an array can only report on content designed into it. Variants not on the chip are not observed and must be inferred by imputation against a reference panel, whose composition determines how well that works, and imputation performs less well for populations poorly represented in available panels. Probes are also sensitive to variants in the probe binding site and to cross-hybridisation of similar sequences, and dynamic range is compressed compared with counting-based methods.

Because the cohort is largely of African ancestry and the panel contains fewer such genomes, imputation accuracy is lower for many variants, and the team restricts analysis to positions meeting an imputation quality threshold.
common_misunderstanding: Array results are sometimes described as sequencing a person's genome. An array does not read sequence; it tests predefined positions by hybridisation. It is therefore blind to any variant not represented on the chip, including most rare variants, and a negative array result is uninformative about positions the design never interrogated.

plain_definition: Contamination control covers the laboratory practices that stop unwanted DNA or RNA entering a reaction or moving between samples. Because amplification and sequencing can detect tiny amounts of material, even invisible traces matter. Measures include separating work areas, using negative controls, handling reagents carefully and watching for suspicious results in the data.
technical_explanation: Contamination in molecular workflows arises from several distinct sources, and the controls differ accordingly. Carry-over of amplified product from previous reactions is the most serious in amplification-based diagnostics and is addressed by unidirectional workflow through physically separate pre-amplification and post-amplification areas, dedicated equipment and, in some assays, enzymatic degradation of previous products. Sample-to-sample cross-contamination during extraction and plate handling is managed by layout design, filtered tips, automation and the deliberate placement of blank wells. Reagent-borne nucleic acid, sometimes called the kit microbiome, is a dominant problem in metagenomics and low-biomass work, where it can generate plausible but spurious taxa. Index misassignment during sequencing creates an analogous effect in the data rather than at the bench. Detection relies on negative and blank controls carried through the whole process, on monitoring the species or variants seen in controls, and on checks of sample identity using independent genotypes. Suspicion should rise when a result appears at very low abundance, when it matches a high-abundance neighbouring sample, or when it appears in controls.

Several bacterial genera appear in both the blanks and the specimens at similar read counts. Treating these as reagent-derived rather than clinical findings, the team removes them from the analysis and reports the limitation alongside the results.
common_misunderstanding: Contamination is often imagined as a visible failure that only careless laboratories experience. Most contamination is invisible and systematic: trace nucleic acid in reagents, aerosols from previous reactions, and index hopping between pooled libraries. Without controls carried through the full process, contamination is indistinguishable from a genuine low-level finding in the data.

plain_definition: The cycle threshold, written Ct, is the number of amplification cycles a quantitative PCR test needs before its fluorescent signal becomes clearly detectable. A sample containing more of the target reaches that point sooner, so a lower cycle threshold indicates more starting material. The value depends on the particular assay and instrument used.
technical_explanation: The cycle threshold, also reported as the quantification cycle, is the fractional cycle number at which amplification signal crosses a defined threshold above background. Under ideal doubling, it is inversely proportional to the logarithm of the initial template concentration, which is the basis of quantification against a standard curve. In practice the value is a property of the whole measurement system: the threshold setting, baseline correction, assay efficiency, target region, reverse transcription step for RNA targets, extraction method and elution volume all shift it. Consequently values are comparable within an assay and laboratory but not between them without calibration to a common standard. In diagnostics the cycle threshold is sometimes used as a proxy for the amount of pathogen material present, and in wastewater surveillance as a relative indicator of community trends, but it reflects the quantity of target nucleic acid in the processed sample rather than infectiousness, viable organism or clinical severity. Sampling quality and the time since onset influence it strongly, so single values carry little interpretive weight.

Falling values across consecutive weeks suggest rising target concentration in the catchment. The programme reports the trend rather than individual values, and normalises against a faecal marker to account for dilution by rainfall.
common_misunderstanding: A cycle threshold is often treated as a direct measure of how much pathogen a person carries, or how infectious they are. It measures target nucleic acid recovered from the processed sample in one specific assay. Sampling technique, extraction and assay design all move the number, and nucleic acid detection does not demonstrate viable organism.

plain_definition: Turnaround time is how long it takes from a sample arriving, or being collected, to a result being issued. In genomics it covers extraction, library preparation, sequencing, analysis, interpretation and reporting. Different parts of that chain dominate for different tests, and a result that arrives too late to inform a decision has limited practical value.
technical_explanation: Turnaround time is a service performance measure defined by the start and end points chosen, so stating them matters: collection to report, receipt to report, and sequencing to data release describe very different intervals. In sequencing workflows the contributions are usually batching delay while enough samples accumulate, library preparation, instrument run time, computational analysis, interpretation by scientific staff, and authorisation. Which step dominates depends on the setting. In high-throughput surveillance, batching and transport often outweigh the run itself; in rare disease diagnostics, interpretation and multidisciplinary review are usually the longest components; in rapid critical care applications, the entire chain is reorganised around speed. Reducing turnaround time involves trade-offs rather than pure gain: smaller batches raise cost per sample, shallower sequencing reduces sensitivity, and compressed interpretation increases the risk of error, so targets should be set against the decision the result informs. Reporting a median alone hides the tail, and it is the delayed minority of cases that usually determines whether a service is clinically or operationally useful.
practical_example: A genomic surveillance programme finds that although its sequencing run takes two days, the interval from sample collection to a shared consensus genome is far longer, because specimens are transported weekly and sequenced in large batches. Moving to more frequent, smaller batches shortens the overall interval, at a higher cost per sample, and makes results useful during an investigation.
common_misunderstanding: Turnaround time is often equated with instrument run time, as though faster sequencing alone would deliver faster results. In most services the laboratory run is a minor component compared with transport, batching, analysis and interpretation. Quoting only the median also conceals the delayed cases, which are usually the ones where timeliness mattered most.

plain_definition: Bioinformatics is the discipline that stores, organises and analyses biological data using computers. Most of that data comes from sequencing DNA, RNA or protein, and it arrives in volumes far too large to inspect by hand. Bioinformatics supplies the file formats, databases, algorithms and statistics that turn raw instrument output into results a biologist, clinician or public health team can actually read and act upon.
technical_explanation: Bioinformatics sits between molecular biology, computer science and statistics. A typical project moves raw sequencing reads through quality control, alignment or assembly, feature counting or variant calling, annotation against reference databases, and statistical testing, with each step writing a standardised file that the next step consumes. Practitioners work mostly on the command line under Unix, scripting in Python, R or shell, and increasingly describe whole analyses in a workflow language so that they can be rerun identically. The discipline also builds and curates the public resources the field depends on, including sequence archives, variant databases and genome browsers. Two limitations deserve emphasis. First, a bioinformatics result is only as good as the reference data behind it: reference genomes, annotation sets and variant frequency databases under-represent many populations, and a tool silently inherits those gaps. Second, software versions, parameter choices and reference builds change results, so an analysis that is not version-controlled and documented cannot be trusted to reproduce. Competence therefore includes data management and reproducibility, not only algorithmic skill.
practical_example: A district laboratory sequences twenty Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from a suspected hospital outbreak. The bioinformatician checks read quality, assembles each genome, screens the assemblies for acquired resistance genes, types the isolates and builds a tree showing which cases cluster together. The laboratory contributes the raw reads and the analysis script to a public archive so that colleagues elsewhere can repeat the work.
common_misunderstanding: Bioinformatics is often treated as a service that begins only after the sequencing is finished, with the analyst handed a folder of files and asked to find something interesting. In practice the analysis plan constrains the experiment: sample numbers, read depth, library type and the handling of batches all have to be settled beforehand, because no algorithm can recover information the design never captured.

plain_definition: FASTQ is the standard text format for raw sequencing reads. Each read occupies four lines: an identifier, the sequence of bases, a separator, and a string of characters encoding how confident the instrument was about each base. Because the quality string travels with the sequence, downstream software can trim or discard unreliable positions rather than treating every base as equally trustworthy.
technical_explanation: A FASTQ record pairs a nucleotide sequence with a per-base quality string of identical length. Each quality character encodes a Phred score as an ASCII character offset by 33 in the encoding now used universally, where the score is minus ten times the logarithm of the estimated probability that the base call is wrong. Files are usually distributed compressed with gzip and are frequently paired, with forward and reverse reads of the same fragment held in matched files in identical order. Public archives distribute submissions in or convert them to this format, so it is the usual entry point to any analysis. Typical first steps are summarising quality by cycle, removing adapter sequence and trimming low-quality tails before alignment or assembly. The main limitations are size and ambiguity: FASTQ files for a human genome run to tens of gigabytes even compressed, and the format carries no structured metadata about the sample, the library or the instrument, so provenance has to be tracked separately. Quality scores are also instrument estimates, not measurements, and can be miscalibrated.
practical_example: Before analysing a batch of SARS-CoV-2 amplicon runs, a surveillance team runs a quality report across all the FASTQ files. One sample shows a sharp drop in quality after cycle 180 and a high proportion of adapter sequence, pointing to a short insert size in that library. The team trims the reads, notes the issue, and flags the sample for a repeat if coverage proves inadequate.
common_misunderstanding: It is tempting to read a FASTQ file as the sample's sequence. It is not: it is a pile of short, redundant, error-containing observations in no particular order, most of which overlap. The consensus or genotype only appears after mapping or assembly, and a base seen in a single read is evidence of very little on its own.

plain_definition: FASTA is a plain-text format for storing sequences. Each record begins with a header line starting with a greater-than sign, followed by the sequence itself on the lines beneath. It is used for reference genomes, gene and protein sequences, assemblies and consensus sequences. Unlike FASTQ, a FASTA record carries no quality information, only the letters of the sequence.
technical_explanation: FASTA is deliberately minimal: a header line introduced by a greater-than sign and then the residues, conventionally wrapped at a fixed line width. Nucleotide records use the IUPAC alphabet, so ambiguity codes such as N or R are legal and common in consensus sequences. Protein records use single-letter amino acid codes. Everything after that sign is free text, which is both the format's convenience and its weakness: identifier conventions differ between databases, and a mismatch between the contig names in a reference FASTA and those in an annotation or variant file is a routine source of pipeline failure. Reference FASTA files are usually accompanied by an index allowing random access to any region without reading the whole file, and by a dictionary used by variant callers. Limitations follow from the simplicity. There is no per-base confidence, no structured metadata and no record of how the sequence was produced, so a consensus with poorly covered regions masked as N looks superficially identical in form to a finished reference. Provenance must be recorded elsewhere.
practical_example: A laboratory submits a consensus genome to a public database and the upload is rejected for exceeding the permitted proportion of ambiguous bases. Inspecting the FASTA shows long runs of N where amplicon dropout left no coverage. The team re-sequences with a revised primer scheme rather than submitting a sequence whose gaps would distort lineage assignment.
common_misunderstanding: A FASTA header is often assumed to be a reliable identifier of what the sequence is. It is only free text written by whoever produced the file, and it is routinely truncated at the first space by downstream tools. Two files whose headers differ in naming style may hold the same chromosomes, and identical headers may hold different genome builds.

plain_definition: SAM and BAM are the standard formats for storing sequencing reads after they have been mapped to a reference genome. SAM is human-readable text; BAM is the same information compressed into a binary file that software can read quickly. Each record says where a read aligned, how well it aligned, and how its bases correspond to the reference at that position.
technical_explanation: A SAM record holds the read name, a bitwise flag describing pairing and orientation, the reference name and leftmost position, a mapping quality, a CIGAR string describing the run-length pattern of matches, insertions, deletions and clipping, the mate's position, the sequence and its quality string, and optional tagged fields used by individual tools. BAM is the compressed binary equivalent; CRAM compresses further by storing differences from the reference rather than the full sequence. Sorted and indexed BAM files allow a viewer or variant caller to retrieve a single locus without scanning the file. Mapping quality is the most misread field: it estimates the probability that the read is placed at the wrong location, not that the bases are correct, and it collapses to zero where a read maps equally well to several places. Reads from repetitive regions, segmental duplications and paralogous genes therefore carry little weight, which is one reason coverage appears uneven across a genome even after a technically successful run.
practical_example: A clinical scientist reviewing a candidate variant opens the BAM file in a genome browser. The supporting reads all align in the same orientation and all carry the alternative allele at the very end of the read, next to a homopolymer run. The pattern suggests an alignment artefact rather than a true variant, so the position is checked by an independent method before it is reported.
common_misunderstanding: Mapping quality and base quality are frequently confused. A read may consist entirely of high-confidence base calls and still have a mapping quality of zero because the region it came from is repeated elsewhere in the genome. Conversely, a uniquely placed read can carry poor base qualities. The two numbers answer different questions and both matter.

plain_definition: Variant Call Format, usually shortened to VCF, is the standard text format for recording differences between sequenced samples and a reference genome. Each line describes one position: where it sits, what the reference carries, what alternative alleles were seen, how confident the caller is, and the genotype of every sample in the file. Annotations and filters are added as extra fields.
technical_explanation: A VCF file has a header of metadata lines defining the reference build, the contigs, and every INFO, FILTER and FORMAT field used, followed by one data line per variant site. Mandatory columns give chromosome, position, identifier, reference and alternative alleles, a quality score, a filter status and a semicolon-separated INFO field; per-sample columns then carry genotype, depth, allele depth and genotype quality under keys declared in FORMAT. Multi-sample VCFs from joint calling allow allele frequencies to be computed across a cohort. BCF is the compressed binary equivalent, and compressed, indexed files permit random access by region. Two cautions matter in practice. The absence of a line does not mean a position matches the reference; it may mean no data were available, which is why a genomic VCF with reference blocks is needed to distinguish a confident reference call from a gap. And representation is not unique: the same insertion or deletion can be written at different positions, so files must be normalised and left-aligned before comparison or merging.

After normalising both VCF files, left-aligning indels and restricting the comparison to regions with adequate coverage in both, nearly all the differences disappear; the remainder sit in a repetitive region where mapping is unreliable.

Standard VCF reports only sites where a variant was called, so an absent position may simply have had no coverage or failed a filter, which is a crucial distinction when a negative result will be reported.

plain_definition: GFF and GTF are text formats that describe where features sit on a genome. Each line gives a sequence name, a start and end coordinate, a feature type such as gene, transcript or exon, a strand, and a set of attributes. They are how a genome assembly, which is only a string of letters, is linked to the biology layered on top of it.
technical_explanation: General Feature Format and its stricter relative Gene Transfer Format both use nine tab-separated columns, differing mainly in how the final attribute column is written. Coordinates are one-based and inclusive, which distinguishes them from BED, a simpler three-to-twelve-column format whose coordinates are zero-based and half-open; converting between the two without adjusting the start coordinate is a standard off-by-one error. Hierarchy is expressed by identifier and parent attributes, so exons point to transcripts and transcripts to genes, allowing alternative isoforms to coexist. Annotation files drive read counting, splice-aware alignment, variant consequence prediction and genome browser displays. Their chief limitation is that annotation is a model, not an observation: gene models differ between Ensembl, RefSeq and project-specific sets, they are revised with every release, and counts or consequences computed against one version are not strictly comparable with another. Contig naming must also match the reference FASTA exactly, since a mixture of naming conventions is a frequent cause of silently empty results.

The reference FASTA uses names such as chr1 while the GTF uses 1, so no feature overlaps any read. Switching to an annotation release matched to the same genome build and naming convention restores the expected counts.
common_misunderstanding: Genome annotation is often read as a settled fact, so that a gene either exists at a locus or does not. Annotation sets are curated models that disagree with one another and change between releases, particularly for non-coding transcripts and alternative isoforms. Reporting the exact annotation source and version is therefore part of reporting the result.

plain_definition: Sequence alignment is the arrangement of two or more sequences so that corresponding positions sit beneath one another, with gaps inserted where one sequence has material the other lacks. It is the basic operation for comparing sequences, and the resulting pattern of matches, mismatches and gaps is the evidence used to infer relatedness, detect variants or identify an unknown sequence.
technical_explanation: Alignment algorithms optimise a score built from substitution rewards and penalties and gap penalties. Global alignment, in the Needleman-Wunsch sense, aligns sequences end to end and suits comparison of complete, similar sequences; local alignment, in the Smith-Waterman sense, finds the best-scoring subregion and suits searching a short query against a large database. Exact dynamic programming is quadratic in sequence length, so practical tools use heuristics: seed-and-extend searching, suffix arrays or the Burrows-Wheeler transform for read mapping, and anchor-based chaining for whole-genome comparison. Multiple sequence alignment extends the problem to many sequences at once and is normally approximated progressively, because the exact solution is computationally intractable; the resulting alignment is the input to phylogenetic inference, so alignment error propagates directly into tree topology. The central limitation is that an alignment is a hypothesis about homology, not an observation of it. Repetitive sequence, large insertions, rearrangements and divergent regions admit several nearly equal-scoring arrangements, and the one reported depends on the scoring parameters chosen.
practical_example: A surveillance team aligns the genomes of an outbreak cluster before building a phylogeny. A region near the end of each genome contains long gaps where coverage was poor, and these gap-rich columns inflate apparent differences between samples. The team masks the unreliable positions from the alignment and rebuilds the tree, which then resolves the cluster sensibly.

Where downstream conclusions depend on a few columns, the alignment itself should be inspected.
